So what is the strangeness in sending someone who warns and admonishes about what will happen in the end, of resurrection and recompense? The pronoun in ﴿But they wonder﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and His saying ﴿and the disbelievers say﴾ is a notice of the reason that makes wonder appropriate, namely that they had been formed upon disbelief, and therefore they wondered. It is also said: the pronoun refers to people in general, because every natural human wonders at a human being being sent as a messenger from Allah. But whoever is granted success looks and is guided and believes, and whoever is forsaken goes astray and disbelieves. They argued with that wonder, and the indication in their saying ﴿This is an amazing thing﴾ is apparently to the coming of a warner from among humans. It is also said it refers to what the warning included, namely the report of resurrection. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is an indication of the return. End of quotation; there is distance in this.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read ﴿أئِذا﴾ with interrogation, following their rules for the second hamza, its softening, and the separation between them. Al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn ʿUtba on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir read إذا with a single hamza in the form of a statement. It is possible that it is an interrogative whose hamza was omitted, and it is possible that they turned to the statement form and omitted the response of إذا, meaning: "When we have died and become dust, we will return." Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ permitted that the response be ﴿a distant return﴾ with the fāʾ omitted. Some permitted that in the response to a condition when it is a nominal sentence, but our companions restricted it to poetry in cases of necessity. As for the reading with interrogation, the adverb (ẓarf) is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Shall we be raised when we have died?" The reference to it is His saying "that," meaning the resurrection.

﴿A distant return﴾, meaning considered unlikely in imaginations and thought. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and idhā is in the accusative governed by an implied element whose meaning is: "When we die and decay, shall we return?" End of quotation. He took this from Ibn Jinnī, who said: it may be that the meaning is: "When we have died after our return," so ﴿a distant return﴾ indicates this verb, and it takes the place of the response to their saying "when?" Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is also possible that "return" means "what is returned to," which is the answer, and that it is part of Allah's speech as a rebuke of their denial of what they were warned about of resurrection; and the pause before it, according to this interpretation, is good. If you ask: what governs the adverb when "return" means "what is returned to"? I say: what the warner indicates from what is warned of, namely the resurrection. End of quotation. That ﴿a distant return﴾ means "what is returned to," and that it is part of Allah's speech and not theirs, as he explained it, is a strange meaning that the Arab understanding does not grasp.

﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾: that is, of their flesh, bones, and traces. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and the majority. This contains a refutation of their considering return unlikely, because whoever knows this is able to return them. Al-Suddī said: that is, what comes into the belly of the earth of their dead. This contains a threat.

﴿And with Us is a recorded book preserved﴾: that is, preserving what is in it, comprehensive, nothing escapes from it, or preserved from decay and change. It is also said that it is an expression for knowledge and enumeration. In a well-established report: the earth consumes the son of Adam except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab), which is a bone like a mustard seed from which the son of Adam is assembled.

﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them﴾: and before this turn (iḍrāb: a shift in the flow of speech) they supposed a clause that this turn is directed against, meaning: they did not consider well, but rather they denied. It is also said: they did not deny the warner, but rather they denied, and the usual pattern is that the iḍrāb occurs after a negated clause. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "But they denied" is an iḍrāb that follows the first iḍrāb, to indicate that they came with something more heinous than their wonder, namely denying the truth, which is the prophethood established by the miracles. End of quotation. This second iḍrāb is a substitute for the first, and both come after that response which we estimated as the answer to the oath, so before the second there is not what they supposed of their saying "they did not consider well." ﴿But they denied the truth﴾. The truth is the Qur'an, or the resurrection, or the Messenger (ﷺ), or Islam, these are opinions. The majority read "when it came to them," meaning they did not reflect on it, but at the first arrival of it they denied. Al-Jaḥdarī read لِما جاءَهم with kasra on the lām and the mīm lightened. Here مَا is a verbal-source particle (ma maṣdariyya), and the lām is the lām of genitive (lām al-jarr), as in the saying of people "I wrote it for five days left," meaning at their coming to it.

﴿Fa-hum fī amrin marīj﴾ (They are in a confused affair). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd said: confused, mixed up. At one time he is a sorcerer, at another a poet, at another a soothsayer. Qatādah said: differing. Al-Ḥasan said: ambiguous. Abū Hurayrah said: corrupt. It is said: "Their trusts (amānāt) became corrupt (marajat amānātu al-nās)," meaning they were spoiled, and "the religion became mixed up (maraja al-dīn)," meaning it was confused. Abū Wāqid said:

> And the religion became confused, so I prepared for it
> A horse with a withers (ḥāriq) that is extended and a chest that is well-knit.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-marīj is the objectionable matter. It is also reported from him: mixed up. The poet said:

> She circled, and I sought her inner parts,
> So she fell as if she were a marīj branch.

The root meaning is agitation and unease. One says: "The ring moved (marija) on my finger," when it became loose from thinness. It is also possible that the marīj affair refers to the shifting of their thoughts concerning what the warner (al-mundhir) brought: first, their non-acceptance of his initial warning to them; then, their astonishment at them; then, their deeming the resurrection (al-baʿth), of which he warned, unlikely; then, their denial of what he brought.

﴿Afa-lam yanẓurū﴾ (Have they not looked), when they disbelieved in the resurrection and in what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, at the signs of the power of God the Exalted in the upper and lower world? ﴿kayfa banaynāhā﴾ (how We built it), raised high without pillars, (and adorned it) with the two luminaries and the stars; ﴿wa-mā lahā min furūj﴾ (and it has no fissures): that is, no breaches or cracks, rather it is sound, free of every flaw.

﴿Wal-arḍa madadnāhā﴾ (And the earth, We spread it out): We extended it. ﴿Wa-alqaynā fīhā rawāsiya﴾ (and We cast into it firm mountains): that is, fixed mountains which keep it from tilting, ﴿min kulli zawjin﴾ (of every kind): that is, type, ﴿bahīj﴾ (beautiful): that is, pleasing to behold, delightful, that gladdens whoever looks at it.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿tabṣiratan wa-dhikrā﴾ (as insight and reminder) in the accusative. Both are in the accusative by an implied verb of their own root, meaning: he gave insight and he reminded. It is said that they are an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi, object of purpose: an accusative noun giving the reason for the action). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read tabṣiratun with the nominative, with dhikrun coordinated to it, meaning: that creation in that description is an insight; and the meaning is that one gains insight by it and is reminded, ﴿li-kulli ʿabdin munīb﴾ (for every servant who turns back): that is, who returns to his Lord and reflects on the wonders of His craftsmanship.

﴿Māʾan mubārakan﴾ (blessed water): that is, abundant in benefit, ﴿wa-ḥabba al-ḥaṣīd﴾ (and the grain of the harvest): that is, the grain that is harvested. This is by omission of the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its place, as the Basrans say. Al-ḥaṣīd is everything that is harvested among what has grain, such as wheat and barley.

﴿Bāsiqāt﴾ (towering): that is, tall in height. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a word describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action), and it is a predicated state (ḥāl muqaddara), because at the time of growth they were not yet tall.  Bāsiqāt is a plural.

﴿Wal-nakhl﴾ (and the palm trees): a collective noun (ism jins). It may be masculine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin munqaʿir﴾ (palm trees uprooted) [al-Qamar: 20]; it may be feminine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin khāwiya﴾ (hollow palm trees) [al-Ḥāqqah: 7]; and it may be plural in view of its singular form, and from this is bāsiqāt, and His saying: ﴿wa-yunshiʾu al-saḥāb al-thiqāl﴾ (and He produces the heavy clouds) [al-Raʿd: 12].

The majority read bāsiqāt with sīn. Quṭbah ibn Mālik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited bāṣiqāt with ṣād. It is a dialect of Banū al-ʿAnbar, who change the sīn into ṣād when it is followed by a khā', ʿayn, qāf or ṭā', or when a letter or two letters separate them.

﴿Lahā ṭalʿ﴾ (it has spathes): its explanation has preceded at His saying: ﴿min ṭalʿihā qinwānun dāniya﴾ (from its spathe, hanging clusters near) [al-Anʿām: 99].

﴿Naḍīd﴾ (layered): that is, piled up, some of it upon the others, meaning the abundance of spathes and their accumulation, that is, the abundance of fruit in them. The first appearance of fruit in the kufurrā (the sheath enclosing the spathe) is white, arranged like pomegranate seeds. As long as it is joined together, one part with another, it is naḍīd; when it comes out of the kufurrā it scatters and is then no longer naḍīd. ﴿Rizqan﴾ (as provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "We caused to grow" is "We provided," or it is an object of purpose.

The majority read ﴿maytan﴾ (dead) with light pronunciation, while Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read it with emphasis. The reference in this is to the revival: that is, the emergence from the earth alive after your death, like that revival of the dead land. All of these are examples and proofs of the resurrection.

He, the Exalted, mentioned three things concerning the sky: the building, the adornment, and the negation of fissures. And concerning the earth He mentioned three: the spreading, the casting of the firm mountains, and the growing of plants. He set the spreading against the building, because spreading is lowering and building is raising. He set the casting of the firm mountains against the adorning with stars, because each of them is anchored. He set the growing, which follows from splitting, against the negation of fissures, so there is no split in it. In what the growing depends on, He alerted to what is harvested every year while its root remains, and what is sown every year or two years and is harvested every year, and to what is mixed from two kinds: some fruits are fruit and not staple food, while most grain is staple food, and fruit is both fruit and staple food.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned His saying: ﴿bal kadhdhabū bil-ḥaqqi lammā jāʾahum﴾ (Rather, they denied the truth when it came to them), He mentioned those who denied the prophets, peace be upon them, as consolation for His Messenger. The discussion of the individual words of this verse and the stories of those mentioned in it has already preceded.

Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Ṭalḥah and Nāfiʿ read ﴿al-ayka﴾ (the Thicket) with the definite article. The majority read ﴿laykah﴾.

﴿Kullun kadhdhaba al-rusul﴾ (each one denied the messengers): that is, all of them, all of them denied. He treated "kull" according to its wording, so He made the pronoun in kadhdhaba singular. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that by it is meant each one of them. End of quote. The tanwīn in "kullun" is the tanwīn of substitution for the omitted genitive noun that it is attached to. Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd, one of the early grammarians of Egypt, permitted dropping the tanwīn from "kullu," making it a final word and building it on a ḍamma, as "qabla" and "baʿda" are built. He thus permitted "kullu" (followed by a verb) "muntaliqan" with a ḍamma on the lām without tanwīn. Al-Akhfash al-Ṣaghīr, who is ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān, rejected this from him.

﴿Fa-ḥaqqa waʿīd﴾ (so the threat was realized): that is, the punishment of the denying nations and their destruction became binding. In this is consolation for the Messenger, and a warning to Quraysh and to whoever denied the Messenger (ﷺ).

**Surah Qaf: forty verses, Meccan**

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is an amazing thing."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust? That is a distant return."﴾ ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a recorded book preserved.﴾ ﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾ ﴿And the earth – We spread it out, placed firm mountains in it, and caused to grow in it every beautiful pair.﴾ ﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾ ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and caused to grow thereby gardens and grain for harvest.﴾ ﴿And tall palm trees with layered clusters of fruit.﴾ ﴿As provision for the servants, and We gave life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence.﴾ ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied, and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud.﴾ ﴿And ʿAd, and Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot.﴾ ﴿And the companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubbaʿ. Each denied the messengers, so My warning came due.﴾ ﴿Were We incapable with the first creation? No, but they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ [Qaf: 15] ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ [Qaf: 16] ﴿When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left.﴾ [Qaf: 17] ﴿He does not utter a word except that there is with him a watcher, ready.﴾ [Qaf: 18] ﴿And the agony of death has come with truth: "This is what you were trying to avoid."﴾ [Qaf: 19] ﴿And the Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the Warning.﴾ [Qaf: 20] ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21] ﴿"You were heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp."﴾ [Qaf: 22] ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ [Qaf: 23] ﴿"Throw into Hell every stubborn disbeliever,﴾ [Qaf: 24] ﴿Preventer of good, transgressor, doubter,﴾ [Qaf: 25] ﴿Who set up with Allah another god, so throw him into the severe punishment."﴾ [Qaf: 26] ﴿His companion will say, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error."﴾ [Qaf: 27] ﴿He will say, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning.﴾ [Qaf: 28] ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants."﴾ [Qaf: 29] ﴿The Day We say to Hell, "Have you been filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30] ﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the righteous, not far away.﴾ [Qaf: 31] ﴿"This is what you were promised, for every one who turns back often and guards [his covenant].﴾ [Qaf: 32] ﴿Who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart returning [in repentance].﴾ [Qaf: 33] ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity.﴾ [Qaf: 34] ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more.﴾ [Qaf: 35] ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in force, so they roamed through the lands – was there any escape?﴾ [Qaf: 36] ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 37] ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ [Qaf: 38] ﴿So be patient over what they say, and exalt your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ [Qaf: 39] ﴿And during part of the night glorify Him, and after the prostrations.﴾ [Qaf: 40] ﴿And listen, the Day the caller calls from a near place.﴾ [Qaf: 41] ﴿The Day they hear the Shout in truth; that is the Day of Coming Out.﴾ [Qaf: 42] ﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.﴾ [Qaf: 43] ﴿The Day the earth splits open from them, rushing; that is a gathering easy for Us.﴾ [Qaf: 44] ﴿We are most knowing of what they say, and you are not over them a compeller. So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.﴾ [Qaf: 45]

Bassaqat al-nakhlatu busuqan: ṭālat (it grew tall). The poet said:
Lanā khamrun wa-laysat khamra karmin / wa-lākin min nitāji l-bāsiqāt
Kirāmin fī s-samāʾi dhahabna ṭūlan / wa-fāta thimāruhā aydī l-junāt

(We have wine, not the wine of a vineyard, but from the produce of the towering ones, noble in the sky, which went up in height, and whose fruit escaped the hands of the pickers.)

Wa-basaqa fulānun ʿalā aṣḥābihi: ayy ʿalāhum (so-and-so towered over his companions, i.e., rose above them). From this is the saying of Ibn Nawfal about Ibn Hubayra:
Yā ibna lladhīna bi-majdihim / basaqat ʿalā Qaysin Fazāra

(O son of those whose glory towered over Qays and Fazara.) (p-119)

It is said: basaqat al-shāt means she gave birth; absaqat al-nāqa means the colostrum appeared in her udder before giving birth, so she is mubsiq, and the camels are mabāsiq. Ḥāda ʿan al-shayʾ: māla ʿanhu, ḥuyūdan wa-ḥaydatan wa-ḥaydūdatan. Al-warīd: a large vein in the neck. It is said there are two veins, one on the right and one on the left. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is what lies between the windpipe (ḥulqūm) and the two ʿilbāwayn (the two ridges beside the neck). Al-Athram said: it is the river of the body; in the heart it is the waṭīn, in the back the abhar, in the arm and thigh the akḥal and the nasā, and in the little finger the aslam. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the two warīd are two veins flanking the two sides of the neck at its front, connected to the waṭīn, coming from the head down to it; it was named warīd because the spirit comes to it (tarid). He said:
Ka-anna wariday-hi ri shāʾun ṣulub
(As if his two jugulars were a hard rope.)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ [the verses are repeated as above] ﴿...so My warning came due.﴾

(p-120) This sura is Meccan. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: by the consensus of the exegetes. The author of al-Taḥrīr said: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda said: it is Meccan except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Qaf: 38], the verse. Its connection to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, informed that those who said "We have believed" did not have true faith, and the absence of their faith is evidence of their denial of the Messenger's prophethood (ﷺ), so He said: ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾. The absence of faith also indicates denial of resurrection, so He followed it with that.

Qaf is a letter of the alphabet (ḥarf hijāʾ: one of the disjointed letters at the beginning of some suras). The exegetes disagreed about its meaning in eleven conflicting opinions, none of which has evidence for its correctness, so I have discarded their transmission in this book.

﴿And the Qur'an﴾ is the object of the oath, and ﴿the glorious﴾ is its attribute, meaning noble above other books. The response is omitted, indicated by what follows it, and its estimate is: that you came to them as a warner of the resurrection, and they did not accept.

﴿But they wonder﴾. It is said: they did not refute your matter with proof. Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and al-Zajjāj said: its estimate is "you will certainly be resurrected." It is also said: the response is mentioned. According to al-Akhfash: ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾. According to Ibn Kaysān and al-Akhfash: ﴿what comes forth from a word﴾. According to the grammarians of Kufa: "But they wonder," meaning "They have indeed wondered." It is also said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾, which is the choice of Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī. It is also said: ﴿What is changed of the word with Me﴾. All these opinions are weak.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read قافْ with the fāʾ sukūn. ʿĪsā read it with fatḥa, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Abū l-Sammāl with kasra, and Hārūn, Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and also al-Ḥasan read it with ḍamma, as transmitted by Ibn Khālawayh. The original form of letters of the alphabet, when not combined with a governing word, is to be pausal (mawqūfa). Whoever reads it with fatḥa has moved to the vowels; whoever reads it with kasra is following the original rule of meeting two unvowelled letters; whoever reads it with ḍamma does so as in the cases of قَطُّ and مُنْذُ and حَيْثُ.

﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾: this is a denial of their wonder at what is not wonderful, namely that a man from among them, whose truthfulness, trustworthiness, and sincerity they knew, should warn them of the fear (of Allah). It would have been appropriate for them not to wonder, especially since they acknowledge Allah's power. So what is the strangeness in sending someone who warns and admonishes about what will happen in the end, of resurrection and recompense? The pronoun in ﴿But they wonder﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and His saying ﴿and the disbelievers say﴾ is a notice of the reason that makes wonder appropriate, namely that they had been formed upon disbelief, and therefore they wondered. It is also said: the pronoun refers to people in general, because every natural human wonders at a human being being sent as a messenger from Allah. But whoever is granted success looks and is guided and believes, and whoever is forsaken goes astray and disbelieves. They argued with that wonder, and the indication in their saying ﴿This is an amazing thing﴾ is apparently to the coming of a warner from among humans. It is also said it refers to what the warning included, namely the report of resurrection. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is an indication of the return. End of quotation; there is distance in this.

Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ permitted that the response be ﴿a distant return﴾ with the fāʾ omitted. Some permitted that in the response to a condition when it is a nominal sentence, but our companions restricted it to poetry in cases of necessity. As for the reading with interrogation, the adverb (ẓarf) is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Shall we be raised when we have died?" The reference to it is His saying "that," meaning the resurrection.

﴿A distant return﴾, meaning considered unlikely in imaginations and thought. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and idhā is in the accusative governed by an implied element whose meaning is: "When we die and decay, shall we return?" End of quotation. He took this from Ibn Jinnī, who said: it may be that the meaning is: "When we have died after our return," so ﴿a distant return﴾ indicates this verb, and it takes the place of the response to their saying "when?" Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is also possible that "return" means "what is returned to," which is the answer, and that it is part of Allah's speech as a rebuke of their denial of what they were warned about of resurrection; and the pause before it, according to this interpretation, is good. If you ask: what governs the adverb when "return" means "what is returned to"? I say: what the warner indicates from what is warned of, namely the resurrection. End of quotation. That ﴿a distant return﴾ means "what is returned to," and that it is part of Allah's speech and not theirs, as he explained it, is a strange meaning that the Arab understanding does not grasp.

﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾: that is, of their flesh, bones, and traces. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and the majority. This contains a refutation of their considering return unlikely, because whoever knows this is able to return them. Al-Suddī said: that is, what comes into the belly of the earth of their dead. This contains a threat.

﴿And with Us is a recorded book preserved﴾: that is, preserving what is in it, comprehensive, nothing escapes from it, or preserved from decay and change. It is also said that it is an expression for knowledge and enumeration. In a well-established report: the earth consumes the son of Adam except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab), which is a bone like a mustard seed from which the son of Adam is assembled.

﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them﴾: and before this turn (iḍrāb: a shift in the flow of speech) they supposed a clause that this turn is directed against, meaning: they did not consider well, but rather they denied. It is also said: they did not deny the warner, but rather they denied, and the usual pattern is that the iḍrāb occurs after a negated clause. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "But they denied" is an iḍrāb that follows the first iḍrāb, to indicate that they came with something more heinous than their wonder, namely denying the truth, which is the prophethood established by the miracles. End of quotation. This second iḍrāb is a substitute for the first, and both come after that response which we estimated as the answer to the oath, so before the second there is not what they supposed of their saying "they did not consider well." ﴿But they denied the truth﴾. The truth is the Qur'an, or the resurrection, or the Messenger (ﷺ), or Islam, these are opinions. The majority read "when it came to them," meaning they did not reflect on it, but at the first arrival of it they denied. Al-Jaḥdarī read لِما جاءَهم with kasra on the lām and the mīm lightened. Here مَا is a verbal-source particle (ma maṣdariyya), and the lām is the lām of genitive (lām al-jarr), as in the saying of people "I wrote it for five days left," meaning at their coming to it.

﴿Fa-hum fī amrin marīj﴾ (They are in a confused affair). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd said: confused, mixed up. At one time he is a sorcerer, at another a poet, at another a soothsayer. Qatādah said: differing. Al-Ḥasan said: ambiguous. Abū Hurayrah said: corrupt. It is said: "Their trusts (amānāt) became corrupt (marajat amānātu al-nās)," meaning they were spoiled, and "the religion became mixed up (maraja al-dīn)," meaning it was confused. Abū Wāqid said:

> And the religion became confused, so I prepared for it
> A horse with a withers (ḥāriq) that is extended and a chest that is well-knit.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-marīj is the objectionable matter. It is also reported from him: mixed up. The poet said:

> She circled, and I sought her inner parts,
> So she fell as if she were a marīj branch.

The root meaning is agitation and unease. One says: "The ring moved (marija) on my finger," when it became loose from thinness. It is also possible that the marīj affair refers to the shifting of their thoughts concerning what the warner (al-mundhir) brought: first, their non-acceptance of his initial warning to them; then, their astonishment at them; then, their deeming the resurrection (al-baʿth), of which he warned, unlikely; then, their denial of what he brought.

﴿Afa-lam yanẓurū﴾ (Have they not looked), when they disbelieved in the resurrection and in what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, at the signs of the power of God the Exalted in the upper and lower world? ﴿kayfa banaynāhā﴾ (how We built it), raised high without pillars, (and adorned it) with the two luminaries and the stars; ﴿wa-mā lahā min furūj﴾ (and it has no fissures): that is, no breaches or cracks, rather it is sound, free of every flaw.

﴿Wal-arḍa madadnāhā﴾ (And the earth, We spread it out): We extended it. ﴿Wa-alqaynā fīhā rawāsiya﴾ (and We cast into it firm mountains): that is, fixed mountains which keep it from tilting, ﴿min kulli zawjin﴾ (of every kind): that is, type, ﴿bahīj﴾ (beautiful): that is, pleasing to behold, delightful, that gladdens whoever looks at it.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿tabṣiratan wa-dhikrā﴾ (as insight and reminder) in the accusative. Both are in the accusative by an implied verb of their own root, meaning: he gave insight and he reminded. It is said that they are an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi, object of purpose: an accusative noun giving the reason for the action). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read tabṣiratun with the nominative, with dhikrun coordinated to it, meaning: that creation in that description is an insight; and the meaning is that one gains insight by it and is reminded, ﴿li-kulli ʿabdin munīb﴾ (for every servant who turns back): that is, who returns to his Lord and reflects on the wonders of His craftsmanship.

﴿Māʾan mubārakan﴾ (blessed water): that is, abundant in benefit, ﴿wa-ḥabba al-ḥaṣīd﴾ (and the grain of the harvest): that is, the grain that is harvested. This is by omission of the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its place, as the Basrans say. Al-ḥaṣīd is everything that is harvested among what has grain, such as wheat and barley.

﴿Bāsiqāt﴾ (towering): that is, tall in height. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a word describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action), and it is a predicated state (ḥāl muqaddara), because at the time of growth they were not yet tall.  Bāsiqāt is a plural.

﴿Wal-nakhl﴾ (and the palm trees): a collective noun (ism jins). It may be masculine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin munqaʿir﴾ (palm trees uprooted) [al-Qamar: 20]; it may be feminine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin khāwiya﴾ (hollow palm trees) [al-Ḥāqqah: 7]; and it may be plural in view of its singular form, and from this is bāsiqāt, and His saying: ﴿wa-yunshiʾu al-saḥāb al-thiqāl﴾ (and He produces the heavy clouds) [al-Raʿd: 12].

The majority read bāsiqāt with sīn. Quṭbah ibn Mālik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited bāṣiqāt with ṣād. It is a dialect of Banū al-ʿAnbar, who change the sīn into ṣād when it is followed by a khā', ʿayn, qāf or ṭā', or when a letter or two letters separate them.

﴿Lahā ṭalʿ﴾ (it has spathes): its explanation has preceded at His saying: ﴿min ṭalʿihā qinwānun dāniya﴾ (from its spathe, hanging clusters near) [al-Anʿām: 99].

﴿Naḍīd﴾ (layered): that is, piled up, some of it upon the others, meaning the abundance of spathes and their accumulation, that is, the abundance of fruit in them. The first appearance of fruit in the kufurrā (the sheath enclosing the spathe) is white, arranged like pomegranate seeds. As long as it is joined together, one part with another, it is naḍīd; when it comes out of the kufurrā it scatters and is then no longer naḍīd. ﴿Rizqan﴾ (as provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "We caused to grow" is "We provided," or it is an object of purpose.

The majority read ﴿maytan﴾ (dead) with light pronunciation, while Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read it with emphasis. The reference in this is to the revival: that is, the emergence from the earth alive after your death, like that revival of the dead land. All of these are examples and proofs of the resurrection.

He, the Exalted, mentioned three things concerning the sky: the building, the adornment, and the negation of fissures. And concerning the earth He mentioned three: the spreading, the casting of the firm mountains, and the growing of plants. He set the spreading against the building, because spreading is lowering and building is raising. He set the casting of the firm mountains against the adorning with stars, because each of them is anchored. He set the growing, which follows from splitting, against the negation of fissures, so there is no split in it. In what the growing depends on, He alerted to what is harvested every year while its root remains, and what is sown every year or two years and is harvested every year, and to what is mixed from two kinds: some fruits are fruit and not staple food, while most grain is staple food, and fruit is both fruit and staple food.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned His saying: ﴿bal kadhdhabū bil-ḥaqqi lammā jāʾahum﴾ (Rather, they denied the truth when it came to them), He mentioned those who denied the prophets, peace be upon them, as consolation for His Messenger. The discussion of the individual words of this verse and the stories of those mentioned in it has already preceded.

Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Ṭalḥah and Nāfiʿ read ﴿al-ayka﴾ (the Thicket) with the definite article. The majority read ﴿laykah﴾.

﴿Kullun kadhdhaba al-rusul﴾ (each one denied the messengers): that is, all of them, all of them denied. He treated "kull" according to its wording, so He made the pronoun in kadhdhaba singular. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that by it is meant each one of them. End of quote. The tanwīn in "kullun" is the tanwīn of substitution for the omitted genitive noun that it is attached to. Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd, one of the early grammarians of Egypt, permitted dropping the tanwīn from "kullu," making it a final word and building it on a ḍamma, as "qabla" and "baʿda" are built. He thus permitted "kullu" (followed by a verb) "muntaliqan" with a ḍamma on the lām without tanwīn. Al-Akhfash al-Ṣaghīr, who is ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān, rejected this from him.

﴿Fa-ḥaqqa waʿīd﴾ (so the threat was realized): that is, the punishment of the denying nations and their destruction became binding. In this is consolation for the Messenger, and a warning to Quraysh and to whoever denied the Messenger (ﷺ).

**Surah Qaf: forty verses, Meccan**

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is an amazing thing."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust? That is a distant return."﴾ ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a recorded book preserved.﴾ ﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾ ﴿And the earth – We spread it out, placed firm mountains in it, and caused to grow in it every beautiful pair.﴾ ﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾ ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and caused to grow thereby gardens and grain for harvest.﴾ ﴿And tall palm trees with layered clusters of fruit.﴾ ﴿As provision for the servants, and We gave life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence.﴾ ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied, and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud.﴾ ﴿And ʿAd, and Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot.﴾ ﴿And the companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubbaʿ. Each denied the messengers, so My warning came due.﴾ ﴿Were We incapable with the first creation? No, but they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ [Qaf: 15] ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ [Qaf: 16] ﴿When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left.﴾ [Qaf: 17] ﴿He does not utter a word except that there is with him a watcher, ready.﴾ [Qaf: 18] ﴿And the agony of death has come with truth: "This is what you were trying to avoid."﴾ [Qaf: 19] ﴿And the Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the Warning.﴾ [Qaf: 20] ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21] ﴿"You were heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp."﴾ [Qaf: 22] ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ [Qaf: 23] ﴿"Throw into Hell every stubborn disbeliever,﴾ [Qaf: 24] ﴿Preventer of good, transgressor, doubter,﴾ [Qaf: 25] ﴿Who set up with Allah another god, so throw him into the severe punishment."﴾ [Qaf: 26] ﴿His companion will say, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error."﴾ [Qaf: 27] ﴿He will say, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning.﴾ [Qaf: 28] ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants."﴾ [Qaf: 29] ﴿The Day We say to Hell, "Have you been filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30] ﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the righteous, not far away.﴾ [Qaf: 31] ﴿"This is what you were promised, for every one who turns back often and guards [his covenant].﴾ [Qaf: 32] ﴿Who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart returning [in repentance].﴾ [Qaf: 33] ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity.﴾ [Qaf: 34] ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more.﴾ [Qaf: 35] ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in force, so they roamed through the lands – was there any escape?﴾ [Qaf: 36] ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 37] ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ [Qaf: 38] ﴿So be patient over what they say, and exalt your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ [Qaf: 39] ﴿And during part of the night glorify Him, and after the prostrations.﴾ [Qaf: 40] ﴿And listen, the Day the caller calls from a near place.﴾ [Qaf: 41] ﴿The Day they hear the Shout in truth; that is the Day of Coming Out.﴾ [Qaf: 42] ﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.﴾ [Qaf: 43] ﴿The Day the earth splits open from them, rushing; that is a gathering easy for Us.﴾ [Qaf: 44] ﴿We are most knowing of what they say, and you are not over them a compeller. So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.﴾ [Qaf: 45]

Bassaqat al-nakhlatu busuqan: ṭālat (it grew tall). The poet said:
Lanā khamrun wa-laysat khamra karmin / wa-lākin min nitāji l-bāsiqāt
Kirāmin fī s-samāʾi dhahabna ṭūlan / wa-fāta thimāruhā aydī l-junāt

(We have wine, not the wine of a vineyard, but from the produce of the towering ones, noble in the sky, which went up in height, and whose fruit escaped the hands of the pickers.)

Wa-basaqa fulānun ʿalā aṣḥābihi: ayy ʿalāhum (so-and-so towered over his companions, i.e., rose above them). From this is the saying of Ibn Nawfal about Ibn Hubayra:
Yā ibna lladhīna bi-majdihim / basaqat ʿalā Qaysin Fazāra

(O son of those whose glory towered over Qays and Fazara.) (p-119)

It is said: basaqat al-shāt means she gave birth; absaqat al-nāqa means the colostrum appeared in her udder before giving birth, so she is mubsiq, and the camels are mabāsiq. Ḥāda ʿan al-shayʾ: māla ʿanhu, ḥuyūdan wa-ḥaydatan wa-ḥaydūdatan. Al-warīd: a large vein in the neck. It is said there are two veins, one on the right and one on the left. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is what lies between the windpipe (ḥulqūm) and the two ʿilbāwayn (the two ridges beside the neck). Al-Athram said: it is the river of the body; in the heart it is the waṭīn, in the back the abhar, in the arm and thigh the akḥal and the nasā, and in the little finger the aslam. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the two warīd are two veins flanking the two sides of the neck at its front, connected to the waṭīn, coming from the head down to it; it was named warīd because the spirit comes to it (tarid). He said:
Ka-anna wariday-hi ri shāʾun ṣulub
(As if his two jugulars were a hard rope.)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ [the verses are repeated as above] ﴿...so My warning came due.﴾

(p-120) This sura is Meccan. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: by the consensus of the exegetes. The author of al-Taḥrīr said: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda said: it is Meccan except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Qaf: 38], the verse. Its connection to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, informed that those who said "We have believed" did not have true faith, and the absence of their faith is evidence of their denial of the Messenger's prophethood (ﷺ), so He said: ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾. The absence of faith also indicates denial of resurrection, so He followed it with that.

Qaf is a letter of the alphabet (ḥarf hijāʾ: one of the disjointed letters at the beginning of some suras). The exegetes disagreed about its meaning in eleven conflicting opinions, none of which has evidence for its correctness, so I have discarded their transmission in this book.

﴿And the Qur'an﴾ is the object of the oath, and ﴿the glorious﴾ is its attribute, meaning noble above other books. The response is omitted, indicated by what follows it, and its estimate is: that you came to them as a warner of the resurrection, and they did not accept.

﴿But they wonder﴾. It is said: they did not refute your matter with proof. Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and al-Zajjāj said: its estimate is "you will certainly be resurrected." It is also said: the response is mentioned. According to al-Akhfash: ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾. According to Ibn Kaysān and al-Akhfash: ﴿what comes forth from a word﴾. According to the grammarians of Kufa: "But they wonder," meaning "They have indeed wondered." It is also said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾, which is the choice of Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī. It is also said: ﴿What is changed of the word with Me﴾. All these opinions are weak.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read قافْ with the fāʾ sukūn. ʿĪsā read it with fatḥa, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Abū l-Sammāl with kasra, and Hārūn, Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and also al-Ḥasan read it with ḍamma, as transmitted by Ibn Khālawayh. The original form of letters of the alphabet, when not combined with a governing word, is to be pausal (mawqūfa). Whoever reads it with fatḥa has moved to the vowels; whoever reads it with kasra is following the original rule of meeting two unvowelled letters; whoever reads it with ḍamma does so as in the cases of قَطُّ and مُنْذُ and حَيْثُ.

﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾: this is a denial of their wonder at what is not wonderful, namely that a man from among them, whose truthfulness, trustworthiness, and sincerity they knew, should warn them of the fear (of Allah). It would have been appropriate for them not to wonder, especially since they acknowledge Allah's power. So what is the strangeness in sending someone who warns and admonishes about what will happen in the end, of resurrection and recompense? The pronoun in ﴿But they wonder﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and His saying ﴿and the disbelievers say﴾ is a notice of the reason that makes wonder appropriate, namely that they had been formed upon disbelief, and therefore they wondered. It is also said: the pronoun refers to people in general, because every natural human wonders at a human being being sent as a messenger from Allah. But whoever is granted success looks and is guided and believes, and whoever is forsaken goes astray and disbelieves. They argued with that wonder, and the indication in their saying ﴿This is an amazing thing﴾ is apparently to the coming of a warner from among humans. It is also said it refers to what the warning included, namely the report of resurrection. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is an indication of the return. End of quotation; there is distance in this.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read ﴿أئِذا﴾ with interrogation, following their rules for the second hamza, its softening, and the separation between them. Al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn ʿUtba on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir read إذا with a single hamza in the form of a statement. It is possible that it is an interrogative whose hamza was omitted, and it is possible that they turned to the statement form and omitted the response of إذا, meaning: "When we have died and become dust, we will return." Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ permitted that the response be ﴿a distant return﴾ with the fāʾ omitted. Some permitted that in the response to a condition when it is a nominal sentence, but our companions restricted it to poetry in cases of necessity. As for the reading with interrogation, the adverb (ẓarf) is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Shall we be raised when we have died?" The reference to it is His saying "that," meaning the resurrection.

﴿A distant return﴾, meaning considered unlikely in imaginations and thought. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and idhā is in the accusative governed by an implied element whose meaning is: "When we die and decay, shall we return?" End of quotation. He took this from Ibn Jinnī, who said: it may be that the meaning is: "When we have died after our return," so ﴿a distant return﴾ indicates this verb, and it takes the place of the response to their saying "when?" Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is also possible that "return" means "what is returned to," which is the answer, and that it is part of Allah's speech as a rebuke of their denial of what they were warned about of resurrection; and the pause before it, according to this interpretation, is good. If you ask: what governs the adverb when "return" means "what is returned to"? I say: what the warner indicates from what is warned of, namely the resurrection. End of quotation. That ﴿a distant return﴾ means "what is returned to," and that it is part of Allah's speech and not theirs, as he explained it, is a strange meaning that the Arab understanding does not grasp.

﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾: that is, of their flesh, bones, and traces. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and the majority. This contains a refutation of their considering return unlikely, because whoever knows this is able to return them. Al-Suddī said: that is, what comes into the belly of the earth of their dead. This contains a threat.

﴿And with Us is a recorded book preserved﴾: that is, preserving what is in it, comprehensive, nothing escapes from it, or preserved from decay and change. It is also said that it is an expression for knowledge and enumeration. In a well-established report: the earth consumes the son of Adam except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab), which is a bone like a mustard seed from which the son of Adam is assembled.

﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them﴾: and before this turn (iḍrāb: a shift in the flow of speech) they supposed a clause that this turn is directed against, meaning: they did not consider well, but rather they denied. It is also said: they did not deny the warner, but rather they denied, and the usual pattern is that the iḍrāb occurs after a negated clause. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "But they denied" is an iḍrāb that follows the first iḍrāb, to indicate that they came with something more heinous than their wonder, namely denying the truth, which is the prophethood established by the miracles. End of quotation. This second iḍrāb is a substitute for the first, and both come after that response which we estimated as the answer to the oath, so before the second there is not what they supposed of their saying "they did not consider well." ﴿But they denied the truth﴾. The truth is the Qur'an, or the resurrection, or the Messenger (ﷺ), or Islam, these are opinions. The majority read "when it came to them," meaning they did not reflect on it, but at the first arrival of it they denied. Al-Jaḥdarī read لِما جاءَهم with kasra on the lām and the mīm lightened. Here مَا is a verbal-source particle (ma maṣdariyya), and the lām is the lām of genitive (lām al-jarr), as in the saying of people "I wrote it for five days left," meaning at their coming to it.

﴿Fa-hum fī amrin marīj﴾ (They are in a confused affair). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd said: confused, mixed up. At one time he is a sorcerer, at another a poet, at another a soothsayer. Qatādah said: differing. Al-Ḥasan said: ambiguous. Abū Hurayrah said: corrupt. It is said: "Their trusts (amānāt) became corrupt (marajat amānātu al-nās)," meaning they were spoiled, and "the religion became mixed up (maraja al-dīn)," meaning it was confused. Abū Wāqid said:

> And the religion became confused, so I prepared for it
> A horse with a withers (ḥāriq) that is extended and a chest that is well-knit.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-marīj is the objectionable matter. It is also reported from him: mixed up. The poet said:

> She circled, and I sought her inner parts,
> So she fell as if she were a marīj branch.

The root meaning is agitation and unease. One says: "The ring moved (marija) on my finger," when it became loose from thinness. It is also possible that the marīj affair refers to the shifting of their thoughts concerning what the warner (al-mundhir) brought: first, their non-acceptance of his initial warning to them; then, their astonishment at them; then, their deeming the resurrection (al-baʿth), of which he warned, unlikely; then, their denial of what he brought.

﴿Afa-lam yanẓurū﴾ (Have they not looked), when they disbelieved in the resurrection and in what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, at the signs of the power of God the Exalted in the upper and lower world? ﴿kayfa banaynāhā﴾ (how We built it), raised high without pillars, (and adorned it) with the two luminaries and the stars; ﴿wa-mā lahā min furūj﴾ (and it has no fissures): that is, no breaches or cracks, rather it is sound, free of every flaw.

﴿Wal-arḍa madadnāhā﴾ (And the earth, We spread it out): We extended it. ﴿Wa-alqaynā fīhā rawāsiya﴾ (and We cast into it firm mountains): that is, fixed mountains which keep it from tilting, ﴿min kulli zawjin﴾ (of every kind): that is, type, ﴿bahīj﴾ (beautiful): that is, pleasing to behold, delightful, that gladdens whoever looks at it.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿tabṣiratan wa-dhikrā﴾ (as insight and reminder) in the accusative. Both are in the accusative by an implied verb of their own root, meaning: he gave insight and he reminded. It is said that they are an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi, object of purpose: an accusative noun giving the reason for the action). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read tabṣiratun with the nominative, with dhikrun coordinated to it, meaning: that creation in that description is an insight; and the meaning is that one gains insight by it and is reminded, ﴿li-kulli ʿabdin munīb﴾ (for every servant who turns back): that is, who returns to his Lord and reflects on the wonders of His craftsmanship.

﴿Māʾan mubārakan﴾ (blessed water): that is, abundant in benefit, ﴿wa-ḥabba al-ḥaṣīd﴾ (and the grain of the harvest): that is, the grain that is harvested. This is by omission of the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its place, as the Basrans say. Al-ḥaṣīd is everything that is harvested among what has grain, such as wheat and barley.

﴿Bāsiqāt﴾ (towering): that is, tall in height. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a word describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action), and it is a predicated state (ḥāl muqaddara), because at the time of growth they were not yet tall.  Bāsiqāt is a plural.

﴿Wal-nakhl﴾ (and the palm trees): a collective noun (ism jins). It may be masculine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin munqaʿir﴾ (palm trees uprooted) [al-Qamar: 20]; it may be feminine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin khāwiya﴾ (hollow palm trees) [al-Ḥāqqah: 7]; and it may be plural in view of its singular form, and from this is bāsiqāt, and His saying: ﴿wa-yunshiʾu al-saḥāb al-thiqāl﴾ (and He produces the heavy clouds) [al-Raʿd: 12].

The majority read bāsiqāt with sīn. Quṭbah ibn Mālik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited bāṣiqāt with ṣād. It is a dialect of Banū al-ʿAnbar, who change the sīn into ṣād when it is followed by a khā', ʿayn, qāf or ṭā', or when a letter or two letters separate them.

﴿Lahā ṭalʿ﴾ (it has spathes): its explanation has preceded at His saying: ﴿min ṭalʿihā qinwānun dāniya﴾ (from its spathe, hanging clusters near) [al-Anʿām: 99].

﴿Naḍīd﴾ (layered): that is, piled up, some of it upon the others, meaning the abundance of spathes and their accumulation, that is, the abundance of fruit in them. The first appearance of fruit in the kufurrā (the sheath enclosing the spathe) is white, arranged like pomegranate seeds. As long as it is joined together, one part with another, it is naḍīd; when it comes out of the kufurrā it scatters and is then no longer naḍīd. ﴿Rizqan﴾ (as provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "We caused to grow" is "We provided," or it is an object of purpose.

The majority read ﴿maytan﴾ (dead) with light pronunciation, while Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read it with emphasis. The reference in this is to the revival: that is, the emergence from the earth alive after your death, like that revival of the dead land. All of these are examples and proofs of the resurrection.

He, the Exalted, mentioned three things concerning the sky: the building, the adornment, and the negation of fissures. And concerning the earth He mentioned three: the spreading, the casting of the firm mountains, and the growing of plants. He set the spreading against the building, because spreading is lowering and building is raising. He set the casting of the firm mountains against the adorning with stars, because each of them is anchored. He set the growing, which follows from splitting, against the negation of fissures, so there is no split in it. In what the growing depends on, He alerted to what is harvested every year while its root remains, and what is sown every year or two years and is harvested every year, and to what is mixed from two kinds: some fruits are fruit and not staple food, while most grain is staple food, and fruit is both fruit and staple food.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned His saying: ﴿bal kadhdhabū bil-ḥaqqi lammā jāʾahum﴾ (Rather, they denied the truth when it came to them), He mentioned those who denied the prophets, peace be upon them, as consolation for His Messenger. The discussion of the individual words of this verse and the stories of those mentioned in it has already preceded.

Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Ṭalḥah and Nāfiʿ read ﴿al-ayka﴾ (the Thicket) with the definite article. The majority read ﴿laykah﴾.

﴿Kullun kadhdhaba al-rusul﴾ (each one denied the messengers): that is, all of them, all of them denied. He treated "kull" according to its wording, so He made the pronoun in kadhdhaba singular. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that by it is meant each one of them. End of quote. The tanwīn in "kullun" is the tanwīn of substitution for the omitted genitive noun that it is attached to. Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd, one of the early grammarians of Egypt, permitted dropping the tanwīn from "kullu," making it a final word and building it on a ḍamma, as "qabla" and "baʿda" are built. He thus permitted "kullu" (followed by a verb) "muntaliqan" with a ḍamma on the lām without tanwīn. Al-Akhfash al-Ṣaghīr, who is ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān, rejected this from him.

﴿Fa-ḥaqqa waʿīd﴾ (so the threat was realized): that is, the punishment of the denying nations and their destruction became binding. In this is consolation for the Messenger, and a warning to Quraysh and to whoever denied the Messenger (ﷺ).

**Surah Qaf: forty verses, Meccan**

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is an amazing thing."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust? That is a distant return."﴾ ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a recorded book preserved.﴾ ﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾ ﴿And the earth – We spread it out, placed firm mountains in it, and caused to grow in it every beautiful pair.﴾ ﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾ ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and caused to grow thereby gardens and grain for harvest.﴾ ﴿And tall palm trees with layered clusters of fruit.﴾ ﴿As provision for the servants, and We gave life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence.﴾ ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied, and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud.﴾ ﴿And ʿAd, and Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot.﴾ ﴿And the companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubbaʿ. Each denied the messengers, so My warning came due.﴾ ﴿Were We incapable with the first creation? No, but they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ [Qaf: 15] ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ [Qaf: 16] ﴿When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left.﴾ [Qaf: 17] ﴿He does not utter a word except that there is with him a watcher, ready.﴾ [Qaf: 18] ﴿And the agony of death has come with truth: "This is what you were trying to avoid."﴾ [Qaf: 19] ﴿And the Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the Warning.﴾ [Qaf: 20] ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21] ﴿"You were heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp."﴾ [Qaf: 22] ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ [Qaf: 23] ﴿"Throw into Hell every stubborn disbeliever,﴾ [Qaf: 24] ﴿Preventer of good, transgressor, doubter,﴾ [Qaf: 25] ﴿Who set up with Allah another god, so throw him into the severe punishment."﴾ [Qaf: 26] ﴿His companion will say, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error."﴾ [Qaf: 27] ﴿He will say, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning.﴾ [Qaf: 28] ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants."﴾ [Qaf: 29] ﴿The Day We say to Hell, "Have you been filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30] ﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the righteous, not far away.﴾ [Qaf: 31] ﴿"This is what you were promised, for every one who turns back often and guards [his covenant].﴾ [Qaf: 32] ﴿Who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart returning [in repentance].﴾ [Qaf: 33] ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity.﴾ [Qaf: 34] ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more.﴾ [Qaf: 35] ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in force, so they roamed through the lands – was there any escape?﴾ [Qaf: 36] ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 37] ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ [Qaf: 38] ﴿So be patient over what they say, and exalt your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ [Qaf: 39] ﴿And during part of the night glorify Him, and after the prostrations.﴾ [Qaf: 40] ﴿And listen, the Day the caller calls from a near place.﴾ [Qaf: 41] ﴿The Day they hear the Shout in truth; that is the Day of Coming Out.﴾ [Qaf: 42] ﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.﴾ [Qaf: 43] ﴿The Day the earth splits open from them, rushing; that is a gathering easy for Us.﴾ [Qaf: 44] ﴿We are most knowing of what they say, and you are not over them a compeller. So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.﴾ [Qaf: 45]

Bassaqat al-nakhlatu busuqan: ṭālat (it grew tall). The poet said:
Lanā khamrun wa-laysat khamra karmin / wa-lākin min nitāji l-bāsiqāt
Kirāmin fī s-samāʾi dhahabna ṭūlan / wa-fāta thimāruhā aydī l-junāt

(We have wine, not the wine of a vineyard, but from the produce of the towering ones, noble in the sky, which went up in height, and whose fruit escaped the hands of the pickers.)

Wa-basaqa fulānun ʿalā aṣḥābihi: ayy ʿalāhum (so-and-so towered over his companions, i.e., rose above them). From this is the saying of Ibn Nawfal about Ibn Hubayra:
Yā ibna lladhīna bi-majdihim / basaqat ʿalā Qaysin Fazāra

(O son of those whose glory towered over Qays and Fazara.) (p-119)

It is said: basaqat al-shāt means she gave birth; absaqat al-nāqa means the colostrum appeared in her udder before giving birth, so she is mubsiq, and the camels are mabāsiq. Ḥāda ʿan al-shayʾ: māla ʿanhu, ḥuyūdan wa-ḥaydatan wa-ḥaydūdatan. Al-warīd: a large vein in the neck. It is said there are two veins, one on the right and one on the left. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is what lies between the windpipe (ḥulqūm) and the two ʿilbāwayn (the two ridges beside the neck). Al-Athram said: it is the river of the body; in the heart it is the waṭīn, in the back the abhar, in the arm and thigh the akḥal and the nasā, and in the little finger the aslam. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the two warīd are two veins flanking the two sides of the neck at its front, connected to the waṭīn, coming from the head down to it; it was named warīd because the spirit comes to it (tarid). He said:
Ka-anna wariday-hi ri shāʾun ṣulub
(As if his two jugulars were a hard rope.)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ [the verses are repeated as above] ﴿...so My warning came due.﴾

(p-120) This sura is Meccan. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: by the consensus of the exegetes. The author of al-Taḥrīr said: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda said: it is Meccan except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Qaf: 38], the verse. Its connection to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, informed that those who said "We have believed" did not have true faith, and the absence of their faith is evidence of their denial of the Messenger's prophethood (ﷺ), so He said: ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾. The absence of faith also indicates denial of resurrection, so He followed it with that.

Qaf is a letter of the alphabet (ḥarf hijāʾ: one of the disjointed letters at the beginning of some suras). The exegetes disagreed about its meaning in eleven conflicting opinions, none of which has evidence for its correctness, so I have discarded their transmission in this book.

﴿And the Qur'an﴾ is the object of the oath, and ﴿the glorious﴾ is its attribute, meaning noble above other books. The response is omitted, indicated by what follows it, and its estimate is: that you came to them as a warner of the resurrection, and they did not accept.

﴿But they wonder﴾. It is said: they did not refute your matter with proof. Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and al-Zajjāj said: its estimate is "you will certainly be resurrected." It is also said: the response is mentioned. According to al-Akhfash: ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾. According to Ibn Kaysān and al-Akhfash: ﴿what comes forth from a word﴾. According to the grammarians of Kufa: "But they wonder," meaning "They have indeed wondered." It is also said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾, which is the choice of Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī. It is also said: ﴿What is changed of the word with Me﴾. All these opinions are weak.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read قافْ with the fāʾ sukūn. ʿĪsā read it with fatḥa, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Abū l-Sammāl with kasra, and Hārūn, Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and also al-Ḥasan read it with ḍamma, as transmitted by Ibn Khālawayh. The original form of letters of the alphabet, when not combined with a governing word, is to be pausal (mawqūfa). Whoever reads it with fatḥa has moved to the vowels; whoever reads it with kasra is following the original rule of meeting two unvowelled letters; whoever reads it with ḍamma does so as in the cases of قَطُّ and مُنْذُ and حَيْثُ.

﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾: this is a denial of their wonder at what is not wonderful, namely that a man from among them, whose truthfulness, trustworthiness, and sincerity they knew, should warn them of the fear (of Allah). It would have been appropriate for them not to wonder, especially since they acknowledge Allah's power. So what is the strangeness in sending someone who warns and admonishes about what will happen in the end, of resurrection and recompense? The pronoun in ﴿But they wonder﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and His saying ﴿and the disbelievers say﴾ is a notice of the reason that makes wonder appropriate, namely that they had been formed upon disbelief, and therefore they wondered. It is also said: the pronoun refers to people in general, because every natural human wonders at a human being being sent as a messenger from Allah. But whoever is granted success looks and is guided and believes, and whoever is forsaken goes astray and disbelieves. They argued with that wonder, and the indication in their saying ﴿This is an amazing thing﴾ is apparently to the coming of a warner from among humans. It is also said it refers to what the warning included, namely the report of resurrection. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is an indication of the return. End of quotation; there is distance in this.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read ﴿أئِذا﴾ with interrogation, following their rules for the second hamza, its softening, and the separation between them. Al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn ʿUtba on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir read إذا with a single hamza in the form of a statement. It is possible that it is an interrogative whose hamza was omitted, and it is possible that they turned to the statement form and omitted the response of إذا, meaning: "When we have died and become dust, we will return." Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ permitted that the response be ﴿a distant return﴾ with the fāʾ omitted. Some permitted that in the response to a condition when it is a nominal sentence, but our companions restricted it to poetry in cases of necessity. As for the reading with interrogation, the adverb (ẓarf) is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Shall we be raised when we have died?" The reference to it is His saying "that," meaning the resurrection.

﴿A distant return﴾, meaning considered unlikely in imaginations and thought. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and idhā is in the accusative governed by an implied element whose meaning is: "When we die and decay, shall we return?" End of quotation. He took this from Ibn Jinnī, who said: it may be that the meaning is: "When we have died after our return," so ﴿a distant return﴾ indicates this verb, and it takes the place of the response to their saying "when?" Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is also possible that "return" means "what is returned to," which is the answer, and that it is part of Allah's speech as a rebuke of their denial of what they were warned about of resurrection; and the pause before it, according to this interpretation, is good. If you ask: what governs the adverb when "return" means "what is returned to"? I say: what the warner indicates from what is warned of, namely the resurrection. End of quotation. That ﴿a distant return﴾ means "what is returned to," and that it is part of Allah's speech and not theirs, as he explained it, is a strange meaning that the Arab understanding does not grasp.

﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾: that is, of their flesh, bones, and traces. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and the majority. This contains a refutation of their considering return unlikely, because whoever knows this is able to return them. Al-Suddī said: that is, what comes into the belly of the earth of their dead. This contains a threat.

﴿And with Us is a recorded book preserved﴾: that is, preserving what is in it, comprehensive, nothing escapes from it, or preserved from decay and change. It is also said that it is an expression for knowledge and enumeration. In a well-established report: the earth consumes the son of Adam except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab), which is a bone like a mustard seed from which the son of Adam is assembled.

﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them﴾: and before this turn (iḍrāb: a shift in the flow of speech) they supposed a clause that this turn is directed against, meaning: they did not consider well, but rather they denied. It is also said: they did not deny the warner, but rather they denied, and the usual pattern is that the iḍrāb occurs after a negated clause. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "But they denied" is an iḍrāb that follows the first iḍrāb, to indicate that they came with something more heinous than their wonder, namely denying the truth, which is the prophethood established by the miracles. End of quotation. This second iḍrāb is a substitute for the first, and both come after that response which we estimated as the answer to the oath, so before the second there is not what they supposed of their saying "they did not consider well." ﴿But they denied the truth﴾. The truth is the Qur'an, or the resurrection, or the Messenger (ﷺ), or Islam, these are opinions. The majority read "when it came to them," meaning they did not reflect on it, but at the first arrival of it they denied. Al-Jaḥdarī read لِما جاءَهم with kasra on the lām and the mīm lightened. Here مَا is a verbal-source particle (ma maṣdariyya), and the lām is the lām of genitive (lām al-jarr), as in the saying of people "I wrote it for five days left," meaning at their coming to it.

﴿Fa-hum fī amrin marīj﴾ (They are in a confused affair). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd said: confused, mixed up. At one time he is a sorcerer, at another a poet, at another a soothsayer. Qatādah said: differing. Al-Ḥasan said: ambiguous. Abū Hurayrah said: corrupt. It is said: "Their trusts (amānāt) became corrupt (marajat amānātu al-nās)," meaning they were spoiled, and "the religion became mixed up (maraja al-dīn)," meaning it was confused. Abū Wāqid said:

> And the religion became confused, so I prepared for it
> A horse with a withers (ḥāriq) that is extended and a chest that is well-knit.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-marīj is the objectionable matter. It is also reported from him: mixed up. The poet said:

> She circled, and I sought her inner parts,
> So she fell as if she were a marīj branch.

The root meaning is agitation and unease. One says: "The ring moved (marija) on my finger," when it became loose from thinness. It is also possible that the marīj affair refers to the shifting of their thoughts concerning what the warner (al-mundhir) brought: first, their non-acceptance of his initial warning to them; then, their astonishment at them; then, their deeming the resurrection (al-baʿth), of which he warned, unlikely; then, their denial of what he brought.

﴿Afa-lam yanẓurū﴾ (Have they not looked), when they disbelieved in the resurrection and in what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, at the signs of the power of God the Exalted in the upper and lower world? ﴿kayfa banaynāhā﴾ (how We built it), raised high without pillars, (and adorned it) with the two luminaries and the stars; ﴿wa-mā lahā min furūj﴾ (and it has no fissures): that is, no breaches or cracks, rather it is sound, free of every flaw.

﴿Wal-arḍa madadnāhā﴾ (And the earth, We spread it out): We extended it. ﴿Wa-alqaynā fīhā rawāsiya﴾ (and We cast into it firm mountains): that is, fixed mountains which keep it from tilting, ﴿min kulli zawjin﴾ (of every kind): that is, type, ﴿bahīj﴾ (beautiful): that is, pleasing to behold, delightful, that gladdens whoever looks at it.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿tabṣiratan wa-dhikrā﴾ (as insight and reminder) in the accusative. Both are in the accusative by an implied verb of their own root, meaning: he gave insight and he reminded. It is said that they are an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi, object of purpose: an accusative noun giving the reason for the action). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read tabṣiratun with the nominative, with dhikrun coordinated to it, meaning: that creation in that description is an insight; and the meaning is that one gains insight by it and is reminded, ﴿li-kulli ʿabdin munīb﴾ (for every servant who turns back): that is, who returns to his Lord and reflects on the wonders of His craftsmanship.

﴿Māʾan mubārakan﴾ (blessed water): that is, abundant in benefit, ﴿wa-ḥabba al-ḥaṣīd﴾ (and the grain of the harvest): that is, the grain that is harvested. This is by omission of the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its place, as the Basrans say. Al-ḥaṣīd is everything that is harvested among what has grain, such as wheat and barley.

﴿Bāsiqāt﴾ (towering): that is, tall in height. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a word describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action), and it is a predicated state (ḥāl muqaddara), because at the time of growth they were not yet tall.  Bāsiqāt is a plural.

﴿Wal-nakhl﴾ (and the palm trees): a collective noun (ism jins). It may be masculine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin munqaʿir﴾ (palm trees uprooted) [al-Qamar: 20]; it may be feminine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin khāwiya﴾ (hollow palm trees) [al-Ḥāqqah: 7]; and it may be plural in view of its singular form, and from this is bāsiqāt, and His saying: ﴿wa-yunshiʾu al-saḥāb al-thiqāl﴾ (and He produces the heavy clouds) [al-Raʿd: 12].

The majority read bāsiqāt with sīn. Quṭbah ibn Mālik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited bāṣiqāt with ṣād. It is a dialect of Banū al-ʿAnbar, who change the sīn into ṣād when it is followed by a khā', ʿayn, qāf or ṭā', or when a letter or two letters separate them.

﴿Lahā ṭalʿ﴾ (it has spathes): its explanation has preceded at His saying: ﴿min ṭalʿihā qinwānun dāniya﴾ (from its spathe, hanging clusters near) [al-Anʿām: 99].

﴿Naḍīd﴾ (layered): that is, piled up, some of it upon the others, meaning the abundance of spathes and their accumulation, that is, the abundance of fruit in them. The first appearance of fruit in the kufurrā (the sheath enclosing the spathe) is white, arranged like pomegranate seeds. As long as it is joined together, one part with another, it is naḍīd; when it comes out of the kufurrā it scatters and is then no longer naḍīd. ﴿Rizqan﴾ (as provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "We caused to grow" is "We provided," or it is an object of purpose.

The majority read ﴿maytan﴾ (dead) with light pronunciation, while Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read it with emphasis. The reference in this is to the revival: that is, the emergence from the earth alive after your death, like that revival of the dead land. All of these are examples and proofs of the resurrection.

He, the Exalted, mentioned three things concerning the sky: the building, the adornment, and the negation of fissures. And concerning the earth He mentioned three: the spreading, the casting of the firm mountains, and the growing of plants. He set the spreading against the building, because spreading is lowering and building is raising. He set the casting of the firm mountains against the adorning with stars, because each of them is anchored. He set the growing, which follows from splitting, against the negation of fissures, so there is no split in it. In what the growing depends on, He alerted to what is harvested every year while its root remains, and what is sown every year or two years and is harvested every year, and to what is mixed from two kinds: some fruits are fruit and not staple food, while most grain is staple food, and fruit is both fruit and staple food.

Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Ṭalḥah and Nāfiʿ read ﴿al-ayka﴾ (the Thicket) with the definite article. The majority read ﴿laykah﴾.

﴿Kullun kadhdhaba al-rusul﴾ (each one denied the messengers): that is, all of them, all of them denied. He treated "kull" according to its wording, so He made the pronoun in kadhdhaba singular.
