**Surah Qaf: forty verses, Meccan**

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is an amazing thing."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust? That is a distant return."﴾ ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a recorded book preserved.﴾ ﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾ ﴿And the earth – We spread it out, placed firm mountains in it, and caused to grow in it every beautiful pair.﴾ ﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾ ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and caused to grow thereby gardens and grain for harvest.﴾ ﴿And tall palm trees with layered clusters of fruit.﴾ ﴿As provision for the servants, and We gave life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence.﴾ ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied, and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud.﴾ ﴿And ʿAd, and Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot.﴾ ﴿And the companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubbaʿ. Each denied the messengers, so My warning came due.﴾ ﴿Were We incapable with the first creation? No, but they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ [Qaf: 15] ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ [Qaf: 16] ﴿When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left.﴾ [Qaf: 17] ﴿He does not utter a word except that there is with him a watcher, ready.﴾ [Qaf: 18] ﴿And the agony of death has come with truth: "This is what you were trying to avoid."﴾ [Qaf: 19] ﴿And the Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the Warning.﴾ [Qaf: 20] ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21] ﴿"You were heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp."﴾ [Qaf: 22] ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ [Qaf: 23] ﴿"Throw into Hell every stubborn disbeliever,﴾ [Qaf: 24] ﴿Preventer of good, transgressor, doubter,﴾ [Qaf: 25] ﴿Who set up with Allah another god, so throw him into the severe punishment."﴾ [Qaf: 26] ﴿His companion will say, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error."﴾ [Qaf: 27] ﴿He will say, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning.﴾ [Qaf: 28] ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants."﴾ [Qaf: 29] ﴿The Day We say to Hell, "Have you been filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30] ﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the righteous, not far away.﴾ [Qaf: 31] ﴿"This is what you were promised, for every one who turns back often and guards [his covenant].﴾ [Qaf: 32] ﴿Who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart returning [in repentance].﴾ [Qaf: 33] ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity.﴾ [Qaf: 34] ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more.﴾ [Qaf: 35] ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in force, so they roamed through the lands – was there any escape?﴾ [Qaf: 36] ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 37] ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ [Qaf: 38] ﴿So be patient over what they say, and exalt your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ [Qaf: 39] ﴿And during part of the night glorify Him, and after the prostrations.﴾ [Qaf: 40] ﴿And listen, the Day the caller calls from a near place.﴾ [Qaf: 41] ﴿The Day they hear the Shout in truth; that is the Day of Coming Out.﴾ [Qaf: 42] ﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.﴾ [Qaf: 43] ﴿The Day the earth splits open from them, rushing; that is a gathering easy for Us.﴾ [Qaf: 44] ﴿We are most knowing of what they say, and you are not over them a compeller. So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.﴾ [Qaf: 45]

Bassaqat al-nakhlatu busuqan: ṭālat (it grew tall). The poet said:
Lanā khamrun wa-laysat khamra karmin / wa-lākin min nitāji l-bāsiqāt
Kirāmin fī s-samāʾi dhahabna ṭūlan / wa-fāta thimāruhā aydī l-junāt

(We have wine, not the wine of a vineyard, but from the produce of the towering ones, noble in the sky, which went up in height, and whose fruit escaped the hands of the pickers.)

Wa-basaqa fulānun ʿalā aṣḥābihi: ayy ʿalāhum (so-and-so towered over his companions, i.e., rose above them). From this is the saying of Ibn Nawfal about Ibn Hubayra:
Yā ibna lladhīna bi-majdihim / basaqat ʿalā Qaysin Fazāra

(O son of those whose glory towered over Qays and Fazara.) (p-119)

It is said: basaqat al-shāt means she gave birth; absaqat al-nāqa means the colostrum appeared in her udder before giving birth, so she is mubsiq, and the camels are mabāsiq. Ḥāda ʿan al-shayʾ: māla ʿanhu, ḥuyūdan wa-ḥaydatan wa-ḥaydūdatan. Al-warīd: a large vein in the neck. It is said there are two veins, one on the right and one on the left. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is what lies between the windpipe (ḥulqūm) and the two ʿilbāwayn (the two ridges beside the neck). Al-Athram said: it is the river of the body; in the heart it is the waṭīn, in the back the abhar, in the arm and thigh the akḥal and the nasā, and in the little finger the aslam. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the two warīd are two veins flanking the two sides of the neck at its front, connected to the waṭīn, coming from the head down to it; it was named warīd because the spirit comes to it (tarid). He said:
Ka-anna wariday-hi ri shāʾun ṣulub
(As if his two jugulars were a hard rope.)

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ [the verses are repeated as above] ﴿...so My warning came due.﴾

(p-120) This sura is Meccan. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: by the consensus of the exegetes. The author of al-Taḥrīr said: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda said: it is Meccan except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Qaf: 38], the verse. Its connection to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, informed that those who said "We have believed" did not have true faith, and the absence of their faith is evidence of their denial of the Messenger's prophethood (ﷺ), so He said: ﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾. The absence of faith also indicates denial of resurrection, so He followed it with that.

Qaf is a letter of the alphabet (ḥarf hijāʾ: one of the disjointed letters at the beginning of some suras). The exegetes disagreed about its meaning in eleven conflicting opinions, none of which has evidence for its correctness, so I have discarded their transmission in this book.

﴿And the Qur'an﴾ is the object of the oath, and ﴿the glorious﴾ is its attribute, meaning noble above other books. The response is omitted, indicated by what follows it, and its estimate is: that you came to them as a warner of the resurrection, and they did not accept.

﴿But they wonder﴾. It is said: they did not refute your matter with proof. Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and al-Zajjāj said: its estimate is "you will certainly be resurrected." It is also said: the response is mentioned. According to al-Akhfash: ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾. According to Ibn Kaysān and al-Akhfash: ﴿what comes forth from a word﴾. According to the grammarians of Kufa: "But they wonder," meaning "They have indeed wondered." It is also said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾, which is the choice of Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī. It is also said: ﴿What is changed of the word with Me﴾. All these opinions are weak.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read قافْ with the fāʾ sukūn. ʿĪsā read it with fatḥa, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Abū l-Sammāl with kasra, and Hārūn, Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and also al-Ḥasan read it with ḍamma, as transmitted by Ibn Khālawayh. The original form of letters of the alphabet, when not combined with a governing word, is to be pausal (mawqūfa). Whoever reads it with fatḥa has moved to the vowels; whoever reads it with kasra is following the original rule of meeting two unvowelled letters; whoever reads it with ḍamma does so as in the cases of قَطُّ and مُنْذُ and حَيْثُ.

﴿But they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾: this is a denial of their wonder at what is not wonderful, namely that a man from among them, whose truthfulness, trustworthiness, and sincerity they knew, should warn them of the fear (of Allah). It would have been appropriate for them not to wonder, especially since they acknowledge Allah's power. So what is the strangeness in sending someone who warns and admonishes about what will happen in the end, of resurrection and recompense? The pronoun in ﴿But they wonder﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and His saying ﴿and the disbelievers say﴾ is a notice of the reason that makes wonder appropriate, namely that they had been formed upon disbelief, and therefore they wondered. It is also said: the pronoun refers to people in general, because every natural human wonders at a human being being sent as a messenger from Allah. But whoever is granted success looks and is guided and believes, and whoever is forsaken goes astray and disbelieves. They argued with that wonder, and the indication in their saying ﴿This is an amazing thing﴾ is apparently to the coming of a warner from among humans. It is also said it refers to what the warning included, namely the report of resurrection. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is an indication of the return. End of quotation; there is distance in this.

The reciters: al-Jumhūr read ﴿أئِذا﴾ with interrogation, following their rules for the second hamza, its softening, and the separation between them. Al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn ʿUtba on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir read إذا with a single hamza in the form of a statement. It is possible that it is an interrogative whose hamza was omitted, and it is possible that they turned to the statement form and omitted the response of إذا, meaning: "When we have died and become dust, we will return." Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ permitted that the response be ﴿a distant return﴾ with the fāʾ omitted. Some permitted that in the response to a condition when it is a nominal sentence, but our companions restricted it to poetry in cases of necessity. As for the reading with interrogation, the adverb (ẓarf) is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Shall we be raised when we have died?" The reference to it is His saying "that," meaning the resurrection.

﴿A distant return﴾, meaning considered unlikely in imaginations and thought. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and idhā is in the accusative governed by an implied element whose meaning is: "When we die and decay, shall we return?" End of quotation. He took this from Ibn Jinnī, who said: it may be that the meaning is: "When we have died after our return," so ﴿a distant return﴾ indicates this verb, and it takes the place of the response to their saying "when?" Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is also possible that "return" means "what is returned to," which is the answer, and that it is part of Allah's speech as a rebuke of their denial of what they were warned about of resurrection; and the pause before it, according to this interpretation, is good. If you ask: what governs the adverb when "return" means "what is returned to"? I say: what the warner indicates from what is warned of, namely the resurrection. End of quotation. That ﴿a distant return﴾ means "what is returned to," and that it is part of Allah's speech and not theirs, as he explained it, is a strange meaning that the Arab understanding does not grasp.

﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾: that is, of their flesh, bones, and traces. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and the majority. This contains a refutation of their considering return unlikely, because whoever knows this is able to return them. Al-Suddī said: that is, what comes into the belly of the earth of their dead. This contains a threat.

﴿And with Us is a recorded book preserved﴾: that is, preserving what is in it, comprehensive, nothing escapes from it, or preserved from decay and change. It is also said that it is an expression for knowledge and enumeration. In a well-established report: the earth consumes the son of Adam except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab), which is a bone like a mustard seed from which the son of Adam is assembled.

﴿But they denied the truth when it came to them﴾: and before this turn (iḍrāb: a shift in the flow of speech) they supposed a clause that this turn is directed against, meaning: they did not consider well, but rather they denied. It is also said: they did not deny the warner, but rather they denied, and the usual pattern is that the iḍrāb occurs after a negated clause. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "But they denied" is an iḍrāb that follows the first iḍrāb, to indicate that they came with something more heinous than their wonder, namely denying the truth, which is the prophethood established by the miracles. End of quotation. This second iḍrāb is a substitute for the first, and both come after that response which we estimated as the answer to the oath, so before the second there is not what they supposed of their saying "they did not consider well." ﴿But they denied the truth﴾. The truth is the Qur'an, or the resurrection, or the Messenger (ﷺ), or Islam, these are opinions. The majority read "when it came to them," meaning they did not reflect on it, but at the first arrival of it they denied. Al-Jaḥdarī read لِما جاءَهم with kasra on the lām and the mīm lightened. Here مَا is a verbal-source particle (ma maṣdariyya), and the lām is the lām of genitive (lām al-jarr), as in the saying of people "I wrote it for five days left," meaning at their coming to it.

﴿Fa-hum fī amrin marīj﴾ (They are in a confused affair). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd said: confused, mixed up. At one time he is a sorcerer, at another a poet, at another a soothsayer. Qatādah said: differing. Al-Ḥasan said: ambiguous. Abū Hurayrah said: corrupt. It is said: "Their trusts (amānāt) became corrupt (marajat amānātu al-nās)," meaning they were spoiled, and "the religion became mixed up (maraja al-dīn)," meaning it was confused. Abū Wāqid said:

> And the religion became confused, so I prepared for it
> A horse with a withers (ḥāriq) that is extended and a chest that is well-knit.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-marīj is the objectionable matter. It is also reported from him: mixed up. The poet said:

> She circled, and I sought her inner parts,
> So she fell as if she were a marīj branch.

The root meaning is agitation and unease. One says: "The ring moved (marija) on my finger," when it became loose from thinness. It is also possible that the marīj affair refers to the shifting of their thoughts concerning what the warner (al-mundhir) brought: first, their non-acceptance of his initial warning to them; then, their astonishment at them; then, their deeming the resurrection (al-baʿth), of which he warned, unlikely; then, their denial of what he brought.

﴿Afa-lam yanẓurū﴾ (Have they not looked), when they disbelieved in the resurrection and in what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, at the signs of the power of God the Exalted in the upper and lower world? ﴿kayfa banaynāhā﴾ (how We built it), raised high without pillars, (and adorned it) with the two luminaries and the stars; ﴿wa-mā lahā min furūj﴾ (and it has no fissures): that is, no breaches or cracks, rather it is sound, free of every flaw.

﴿Wal-arḍa madadnāhā﴾ (And the earth, We spread it out): We extended it. ﴿Wa-alqaynā fīhā rawāsiya﴾ (and We cast into it firm mountains): that is, fixed mountains which keep it from tilting, ﴿min kulli zawjin﴾ (of every kind): that is, type, ﴿bahīj﴾ (beautiful): that is, pleasing to behold, delightful, that gladdens whoever looks at it.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿tabṣiratan wa-dhikrā﴾ (as insight and reminder) in the accusative. Both are in the accusative by an implied verb of their own root, meaning: he gave insight and he reminded. It is said that they are an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi, object of purpose: an accusative noun giving the reason for the action). Zayd ibn ʿAlī read tabṣiratun with the nominative, with dhikrun coordinated to it, meaning: that creation in that description is an insight; and the meaning is that one gains insight by it and is reminded, ﴿li-kulli ʿabdin munīb﴾ (for every servant who turns back): that is, who returns to his Lord and reflects on the wonders of His craftsmanship.

﴿Māʾan mubārakan﴾ (blessed water): that is, abundant in benefit, ﴿wa-ḥabba al-ḥaṣīd﴾ (and the grain of the harvest): that is, the grain that is harvested. This is by omission of the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its place, as the Basrans say. Al-ḥaṣīd is everything that is harvested among what has grain, such as wheat and barley.

﴿Bāsiqāt﴾ (towering): that is, tall in height. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a word describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action), and it is a predicated state (ḥāl muqaddara), because at the time of growth they were not yet tall.  Bāsiqāt is a plural.

﴿Wal-nakhl﴾ (and the palm trees): a collective noun (ism jins). It may be masculine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin munqaʿir﴾ (palm trees uprooted) [al-Qamar: 20]; it may be feminine, as in His saying: ﴿nakhlin khāwiya﴾ (hollow palm trees) [al-Ḥāqqah: 7]; and it may be plural in view of its singular form, and from this is bāsiqāt, and His saying: ﴿wa-yunshiʾu al-saḥāb al-thiqāl﴾ (and He produces the heavy clouds) [al-Raʿd: 12].

The majority read bāsiqāt with sīn. Quṭbah ibn Mālik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited bāṣiqāt with ṣād. It is a dialect of Banū al-ʿAnbar, who change the sīn into ṣād when it is followed by a khā', ʿayn, qāf or ṭā', or when a letter or two letters separate them.

﴿Lahā ṭalʿ﴾ (it has spathes): its explanation has preceded at His saying: ﴿min ṭalʿihā qinwānun dāniya﴾ (from its spathe, hanging clusters near) [al-Anʿām: 99].

﴿Naḍīd﴾ (layered): that is, piled up, some of it upon the others, meaning the abundance of spathes and their accumulation, that is, the abundance of fruit in them. The first appearance of fruit in the kufurrā (the sheath enclosing the spathe) is white, arranged like pomegranate seeds. As long as it is joined together, one part with another, it is naḍīd; when it comes out of the kufurrā it scatters and is then no longer naḍīd. ﴿Rizqan﴾ (as provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "We caused to grow" is "We provided," or it is an object of purpose.

The majority read ﴿maytan﴾ (dead) with light pronunciation, while Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read it with emphasis. The reference in this is to the revival: that is, the emergence from the earth alive after your death, like that revival of the dead land. All of these are examples and proofs of the resurrection.

He, the Exalted, mentioned three things concerning the sky: the building, the adornment, and the negation of fissures. And concerning the earth He mentioned three: the spreading, the casting of the firm mountains, and the growing of plants. He set the spreading against the building, because spreading is lowering and building is raising. He set the casting of the firm mountains against the adorning with stars, because each of them is anchored. He set the growing, which follows from splitting, against the negation of fissures, so there is no split in it. In what the growing depends on, He alerted to what is harvested every year while its root remains, and what is sown every year or two years and is harvested every year, and to what is mixed from two kinds: some fruits are fruit and not staple food, while most grain is staple food, and fruit is both fruit and staple food.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned His saying: ﴿bal kadhdhabū bil-ḥaqqi lammā jāʾahum﴾ (Rather, they denied the truth when it came to them), He mentioned those who denied the prophets, peace be upon them, as consolation for His Messenger. The discussion of the individual words of this verse and the stories of those mentioned in it has already preceded.

Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Ṭalḥah and Nāfiʿ read ﴿al-ayka﴾ (the Thicket) with the definite article. The majority read ﴿laykah﴾.

﴿Kullun kadhdhaba al-rusul﴾ (each one denied the messengers): that is, all of them, all of them denied. He treated "kull" according to its wording, so He made the pronoun in kadhdhaba singular. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that by it is meant each one of them. End of quote. The tanwīn in "kullun" is the tanwīn of substitution for the omitted genitive noun that it is attached to. Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd, one of the early grammarians of Egypt, permitted dropping the tanwīn from "kullu," making it a final word and building it on a ḍamma, as "qabla" and "baʿda" are built. He thus permitted "kullu" (followed by a verb) "muntaliqan" with a ḍamma on the lām without tanwīn. Al-Akhfash al-Ṣaghīr, who is ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān, rejected this from him.

﴿Fa-ḥaqqa waʿīd﴾ (so the threat was realized): that is, the punishment of the denying nations and their destruction became binding. In this is consolation for the Messenger, and a warning to Quraysh and to whoever denied the Messenger (ﷺ).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 50, verses 15–21:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Were We then worn out by the first creation? Nay, but they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ ﴿And We have indeed created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ ﴿When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left.﴾ ﴿He utters no word except that with him is a watcher ready.﴾ ﴿And the agony of death has come in truth: "This is what you were trying to avoid."﴾ ﴿And the Horn will be blown: that is the Day of the Promise.﴾ ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾

(p-123) ﴿Were We then worn out by the first creation?﴾: This is the bringing into being of man from a drop of semen in gradual stages. The explanation of ʿayiya (to be worn out, to be unable) has already been given in His saying: ﴿and He was not wearied by their creation﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. The majority read ﴿afaʿayīnā﴾ with a kasra on the first ʿayn-letter (yāʾ) followed by a silent yāʾ, as the past tense of ʿayiya, like raḍiya. Ibn Abi ʿAbla, al-Walid ibn Muslim, al-Qurṣubi on the authority of Abu Jaʿfar, al-Simsar on the authority of Shayba, and Abu Bahr on the authority of Nafiʿ read it with a shaddah on the yāʾ without lengthening the second vowel. This is what Abu al-Qasim al-Hudhali said in his book al-Kamil. Ibn Khalawayh said in his book Shawadhdh al-Qiraʾat: ﴿afaʿayyinā﴾ with a shaddah on the yāʾ. (Ibn Abi ʿAbla's reading is) — and I reflected on how to account for this reading, since no one had mentioned its justification. I explained it according to the dialect of those who assimilate the yāʾ into the yāʾ in the past tense, saying ʿayya for ʿayiya and ḥayya for ḥayiya. When he assimilated it and attached the pronoun of the speaker who magnifies himself, he did not separate the assimilated letters, saying ʿayyinā. This is a dialect of some of the Bakr ibn Wāʾil, who say, for radadtu and radadnā, raddat and raddanā, without separating. According to this dialect the stressed yāʾ is vowelled with a fatḥa. If nā were an object pronoun, the Arabs would have agreed on assimilation, as in raddanā Zayd (Zayd returned us). Al-Hasan said: "The first creation is Adam (peace be upon him)," and the meaning is: "Were We incapable of the first creation, that We would be incapable of the second?" This is a rebuke to the unbelievers, a reproach, and the establishment of a clear proof against them.

﴿Nay, but they are in doubt﴾: that is, confusion, suspicion and bewilderment. From this is the saying of ʿAli: "O neighbour, it has indeed been confused for you; know the truth and you will know its people."

﴿about a new creation﴾: that is, the resurrection from the graves.

﴿And We have indeed created man﴾: these are verses containing the establishment of proofs against the unbelievers in their denial of resurrection. "Man" (al-insān) is a generic noun. It has been said that it refers to Adam.

﴿and We are nearer﴾: nearness of knowledge of him and of his states; nothing of his hidden things is concealed from Him. It is as though His essence were near to him, as one says: "Allah is in every place," meaning by His knowledge, while He is transcendent above places. And ﴿the jugular vein﴾ is a metaphor for extreme nearness, like the Arabs' saying: "He is nearer to me than the midwife's seat," and "than the loincloth's seat." Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"Death is nearer to me than the jugular vein."*

The word ḥabl (here) is the vein that is likened to a single one of the cords (ḥibāl), and its being attached to al-warīd is for specification, as in their saying: "a camel (sāʾiba)." Or it may be intended: "the cord of the shoulder," and it is attached to al-warīd, as it is attached to the shoulder, because they both are in one organ. The governing word of ﴿idh﴾ (when) is ﴿aqrab﴾ (nearer). It has been said: the implied verb is "remember" (udhkur). It has been said that it is good to estimate "remember," because He reported a bare report about the creation, the knowledge of the stirrings of souls, and the nearness by power and dominion. When the report was complete, He reported by mentioning the states that confirm this report and help its reaching the hearer. Among them: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾; and among them the coming of the agony of death; and among them the blowing of the Horn; and among them the coming of every soul with a driver and a witness. ﴿And the agony of death has come﴾: this is coordinated with ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾. ("The agony of death," sakrat al-mawt) is what afflicts a person at the time of his death-struggle. The bāʾ in (bi-l-ḥaqq) is for transitivity, i.e., "the agony of death has brought the truth," which is the matter by which Allah made His books speak and sent His messengers, concerning the happiness or wretchedness of the dead person. Or it is for the state, i.e., "accompanied by the truth." Ibn Masʿud read sakrān in the plural.

﴿"This is what you were trying to avoid"﴾: that is, you were inclining away. You say: "I live thus-and-so and thus-and-so," so whenever he thinks about the nearness of death, he turns his mind away from it and hopes for a far distance of time. From ḥayd (avoidance) is the fear of death. The apparent sense of "you were trying to avoid" is that it is addressed to the person whom the agony of death has come upon. Al-Zamakhshari said: the address is to the wicked. (*taḥīd*): flees, runs away.

﴿That is the Day of the Promise﴾: this is with an omission: i.e., the time of that is the day of the promise. The demonstrative refers to the verbal noun of "blew" (nafakha). He attributed the day to the promise, although it is the day of both promise and threat together, by way of warning.

The majority read ﴿maʿahā﴾ (with it), and Ṭalḥa read it with a heavy ḥāʾ, assimilating the ʿayn into the hāʾ, so both became ḥāʾ, as they said: "dhahaba maḥḥum," meaning maʿahum (they went with them). ﴿driver﴾: one who drives along the way. ﴿witness﴾: one who bears witness against him. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, Mujahid and others said: there are two angels assigned to every person, one of whom drives him, and the other, from his guarding, bears witness against him. Abu Hurayrah said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the Prophet (ﷺ). It has been said: the witness is the book that he will meet opened. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿a driver and a witness﴾ are generic nouns: the driver is angels assigned to that, and the witness is the guardians and everyone who bears witness. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥak said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the limbs of the person. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is far from Ibn ʿAbbas, because the limbs only bear witness to disobedience, and His saying ﴿every soul﴾ includes the righteous, so its meaning is: "and a witness to his good and his evil." The generic sense is stronger for "witness," so the angels and the places bear witness to good, and from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No jinn, no human, and nothing that hears the reach of the muezzin's voice, but it will bear witness for him on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Hurayrah said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the deed. Abu Muslim said: the driver is a devil, but this is a weak view. Al-Zamakhshari said: there are two angels, one of whom drives him to the gathering place, and the other bears witness against him by his deed; or one angel combines both matters, as if it were said: "an angel who drives him and bears witness against him." The place of ﴿maʿahā sāʾiq﴾ is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) from ﴿kull﴾ (every), because it is definite by its being annexed to what is in the position of a definite. This is a worthless statement that does not come from a beginner in grammar, because if "every soul" were qualified, it could only be qualified by an indefinite; so it is indefinite in every case, and "kull" cannot become definite while it is annexed to an indefinite.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 50, verses 15–21:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Were We then worn out by the first creation? Nay, but they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ ﴿And We have indeed created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ ﴿When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left.﴾ ﴿He utters no word except that with him is a watcher ready.﴾ ﴿And the agony of death has come in truth: "This is what you were trying to avoid."﴾ ﴿And the Horn will be blown: that is the Day of the Promise.﴾ ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾

(p-123) ﴿Were We then worn out by the first creation?﴾: This is the bringing into being of man from a drop of semen in gradual stages. The explanation of ʿayiya (to be worn out, to be unable) has already been given in His saying: ﴿and He was not wearied by their creation﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. The majority read ﴿afaʿayīnā﴾ with a kasra on the first ʿayn-letter (yāʾ) followed by a silent yāʾ, as the past tense of ʿayiya, like raḍiya. Ibn Abi ʿAbla, al-Walid ibn Muslim, al-Qurṣubi on the authority of Abu Jaʿfar, al-Simsar on the authority of Shayba, and Abu Bahr on the authority of Nafiʿ read it with a shaddah on the yāʾ without lengthening the second vowel. This is what Abu al-Qasim al-Hudhali said in his book al-Kamil. Ibn Khalawayh said in his book Shawadhdh al-Qiraʾat: ﴿afaʿayyinā﴾ with a shaddah on the yāʾ. (Ibn Abi ʿAbla's reading is) — and I reflected on how to account for this reading, since no one had mentioned its justification. I explained it according to the dialect of those who assimilate the yāʾ into the yāʾ in the past tense, saying ʿayya for ʿayiya and ḥayya for ḥayiya. When he assimilated it and attached the pronoun of the speaker who magnifies himself, he did not separate the assimilated letters, saying ʿayyinā. This is a dialect of some of the Bakr ibn Wāʾil, who say, for radadtu and radadnā, raddat and raddanā, without separating. According to this dialect the stressed yāʾ is vowelled with a fatḥa. If nā were an object pronoun, the Arabs would have agreed on assimilation, as in raddanā Zayd (Zayd returned us). Al-Hasan said: "The first creation is Adam (peace be upon him)," and the meaning is: "Were We incapable of the first creation, that We would be incapable of the second?" This is a rebuke to the unbelievers, a reproach, and the establishment of a clear proof against them.

﴿Nay, but they are in doubt﴾: that is, confusion, suspicion and bewilderment. From this is the saying of ʿAli: "O neighbour, it has indeed been confused for you; know the truth and you will know its people."

﴿about a new creation﴾: that is, the resurrection from the graves.

﴿And We have indeed created man﴾: these are verses containing the establishment of proofs against the unbelievers in their denial of resurrection. "Man" (al-insān) is a generic noun. It has been said that it refers to Adam.

﴿and We are nearer﴾: nearness of knowledge of him and of his states; nothing of his hidden things is concealed from Him. It is as though His essence were near to him, as one says: "Allah is in every place," meaning by His knowledge, while He is transcendent above places. And ﴿the jugular vein﴾ is a metaphor for extreme nearness, like the Arabs' saying: "He is nearer to me than the midwife's seat," and "than the loincloth's seat." Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"Death is nearer to me than the jugular vein."*

The word ḥabl (here) is the vein that is likened to a single one of the cords (ḥibāl), and its being attached to al-warīd is for specification, as in their saying: "a camel (sāʾiba)." Or it may be intended: "the cord of the shoulder," and it is attached to al-warīd, as it is attached to the shoulder, because they both are in one organ. The governing word of ﴿idh﴾ (when) is ﴿aqrab﴾ (nearer). It has been said: the implied verb is "remember" (udhkur). It has been said that it is good to estimate "remember," because He reported a bare report about the creation, the knowledge of the stirrings of souls, and the nearness by power and dominion. When the report was complete, He reported by mentioning the states that confirm this report and help its reaching the hearer. Among them: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾; and among them the coming of the agony of death; and among them the blowing of the Horn; and among them the coming of every soul with a driver and a witness. The two receivers (al-mutalaqqiyān) are the two angels assigned to every person: the angel of the right writes the good deeds, and the angel of the left writes the bad deeds. Al-Hasan said: "The guardians are four: two by day and two by night." And ﴿qaʿīd﴾ (seated) is singular, so it is possible that its meaning is "one who sits (muqāʿid)," as you say jalīs (companion) and khalīṭ (associate), meaning one who sits with and one who mixes with. It is also possible that it is ʿadl (a form shifted) from fāʿil to faʿīl for intensification, like ʿalīm (knowing). The Kufans said: a singular noun is used in place of the dual, and the better view is that there is an omission from the first, because the second indicates it, i.e., "on the right, a seated one," as the poet said:

*"He threw me with a matter of which I and my father were innocent, and for the sake of the well he threw me."*

According to the better of the two interpretations of it, meaning: "I was innocent of it, and my father was innocent." The view of al-Mubarrad is that the estimate is "on the right, a seated one; and on the left," so he delayed qaʿīd from its place. The view of al-Farraʾ is that the word qaʿīd indicates the dual and the plural, so no estimate is needed.

The majority read ﴿whatever word he utters﴾, and the apparent sense of "whatever he utters" is generality. Mujahid and Abu al-Hawraʾ said: everything is written down against him, even his moaning during his illness. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the two write all speech, then Allah, exalted is He, confirms from that the good and bad deeds and erases what is other than that. It has been said: it is specific, i.e., of good or evil speech. ʿIkrimah said the same, and what falls outside this is not written. They differed about the specification of the sitting of the two angels, and nothing authentic is reported about it.

(*raqīb*): an angel who watches. (*ʿatīd*): present, ready. And when it is "a watcher ready" in wording, then it is more fitting in action.

Al-Hasan said: when he dies, his scroll is folded. It has been said: on the Day of Resurrection he will be told, "Read your book."

﴿And the agony of death has come﴾: this is coordinated with ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾. ("The agony of death," sakrat al-mawt) is what afflicts a person at the time of his death-struggle. The bāʾ in (bi-l-ḥaqq) is for transitivity, i.e., "the agony of death has brought the truth," which is the matter by which Allah made His books speak and sent His messengers, concerning the happiness or wretchedness of the dead person. Or it is for the state, i.e., "accompanied by the truth." Ibn Masʿud read sakrān in the plural.

﴿"This is what you were trying to avoid"﴾: that is, you were inclining away. You say: "I live thus-and-so and thus-and-so," so whenever he thinks about the nearness of death, he turns his mind away from it and hopes for a far distance of time. From ḥayd (avoidance) is the fear of death. The apparent sense of "you were trying to avoid" is that it is addressed to the person whom the agony of death has come upon. Al-Zamakhshari said: the address is to the wicked. (*taḥīd*): flees, runs away.

﴿That is the Day of the Promise﴾: this is with an omission: i.e., the time of that is the day of the promise. The demonstrative refers to the verbal noun of "blew" (nafakha). He attributed the day to the promise, although it is the day of both promise and threat together, by way of warning.

The majority read ﴿maʿahā﴾ (with it), and Ṭalḥa read it with a heavy ḥāʾ, assimilating the ʿayn into the hāʾ, so both became ḥāʾ, as they said: "dhahaba maḥḥum," meaning maʿahum (they went with them). ﴿driver﴾: one who drives along the way. ﴿witness﴾: one who bears witness against him. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, Mujahid and others said: there are two angels assigned to every person, one of whom drives him, and the other, from his guarding, bears witness against him. Abu Hurayrah said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the Prophet (ﷺ). It has been said: the witness is the book that he will meet opened. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿a driver and a witness﴾ are generic nouns: the driver is angels assigned to that, and the witness is the guardians and everyone who bears witness. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥak said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the limbs of the person. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is far from Ibn ʿAbbas, because the limbs only bear witness to disobedience, and His saying ﴿every soul﴾ includes the righteous, so its meaning is: "and a witness to his good and his evil." The generic sense is stronger for "witness," so the angels and the places bear witness to good, and from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No jinn, no human, and nothing that hears the reach of the muezzin's voice, but it will bear witness for him on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Hurayrah said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the deed. Abu Muslim said: the driver is a devil, but this is a weak view. Al-Zamakhshari said: there are two angels, one of whom drives him to the gathering place, and the other bears witness against him by his deed; or one angel combines both matters, as if it were said: "an angel who drives him and bears witness against him." The place of ﴿maʿahā sāʾiq﴾ is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) from ﴿kull﴾ (every), because it is definite by its being annexed to what is in the position of a definite. This is a worthless statement that does not come from a beginner in grammar, because if "every soul" were qualified, it could only be qualified by an indefinite; so it is indefinite in every case, and "kull" cannot become definite while it is annexed to an indefinite.

[p. 125] The Almighty and Majestic said: ﴿Certainly you were heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and today your sight is sharp.﴾ ﴿And his companion says, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever,﴾ ﴿hinderer of good, transgressor, doubter,﴾ ﴿who set up another god with Allah, so cast him into the severe punishment.﴾ ﴿His companion says, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error."﴾ ﴿He says, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning.﴾ ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants."﴾ ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Have you been filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ ﴿And Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, not far off.﴾ ﴿"This is what you were promised, for every constantly returning, watchful one,﴾ ﴿who feared the Most Merciful in the unseen and came with a heart turning in repentance.﴾ ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity."﴾ ﴿For them there is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more.﴾ ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in force, and they roamed through the lands; was there any escape?﴾ [Qaf: 36] ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 37] ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.﴾ [Qaf: 38] ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ [Qaf: 39] ﴿And glorify Him during part of the night and after the prostrations.﴾ [Qaf: 40] ﴿And listen on the Day the caller calls from a near place,﴾ [Qaf: 41] ﴿the Day they hear the Shout in truth; that is the Day of coming forth.﴾ [Qaf: 42] ﴿Indeed We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.﴾ [Qaf: 43] ﴿On the Day the earth splits open from them, hastening; that is a gathering easy for Us.﴾ [Qaf: 44] ﴿We know best what they say, and you are not over them a compeller. So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.﴾ [Qaf: 45] And (the commentary moves to) al-Dhariyat.

[p. 126] The majority of readers recited ﴿لَقَدْ كُنْتَ﴾ (kunta, "you were") with a fatha on the ta and the kaf in "كُنْتَ", and in "﴿غِطاءَكَ﴾" and "بَصَرُكَ", whereas al-Jahdari read them with a kasra, addressing the self (nafs). The majority read ﴿عَنْكَ غِطاءَكَ فَبَصَرُكَ﴾ with a fatha on the ta and the kaf, treating it according to the masculine wording of "كُلُّ" (every). Al-Jahdari and Talha ibn Musarrif read عَنْكِ غِطاءَكِ فَبَصَرُكِ with a kasra, also observing the feminine nafs. The author of al-Lawami' (Sahib al-Lawami') reported the kasra on the kaf only from Talha alone. He said: "I did not find it from him in ﴿لَقَدْ كُنْتَ﴾." If the kasra is read, then all of them are one form; and if ﴿لَقَدْ كُنْتَ﴾ is read with a fatha, then it is an interpretation by taking "كُلُّ" as masculine. It is permissible to make "كُلُّ" feminine in this construction because it is annexed to nafs, which is feminine. Even if that is so, he treated part of it according to the wording and part according to the meaning, like His saying: ﴿فَلَهُ أجْرُهُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112], then He said: ﴿وَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62]. End of quote.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Salih ibn Kaysan and al-Dahhak said: it is said to the disbelieving heedless one among those who have a soul accompanied by the driver and the witness, when he is brought before the Most Merciful and sees the realities which he did not believe in during the world and which he neglected to consider: ﴿Certainly you were heedless of this﴾, that is, of the consequence of disbelief. ﴿So when the covering is removed from you, your sight is sharp﴾, that is, your insight is sharp. This is like saying: so-and-so has a sharp mind (ḥadīd al-dhihn). Mujahid said: it is the sight of the eye, meaning his gaze became sharp toward his scale and other terrors of the Resurrection. There is a statement from Zayd ibn Aslam on this verse which it is forbidden to transmit, and it is in the book of Ibn ʿAtiyya. He used "the covering" as a metaphor for heedlessness, as though it covered all of him or his eyes, so he does not see. When he is in the Resurrection, heedlessness departs from him, and he sees what he did not see of the truth.

﴿And his companion says﴾: that is, among the guards of Hell. ﴿This﴾: the punishment that is with me for this disbelieving human. ﴿Ready﴾: present. This statement is made beautiful by the use of "ما" for what does not reason. Qatada said: "his companion" is the angel assigned to driving him, meaning: this disbeliever whom I drive is present with me. al-Zahrawi said: it is also said that "his companion" is his devil, but this is weak, because what is in it is that the companion in His saying ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾ is his devil in the world who misled him, without disagreement. The word "qarin" is a noun of genus, so his driver is a qarin, his companion among the guards is a qarin, and one who walks alongside a person on his path is a qarin. It is said: his companion here is his deed, in heart and limbs. al-Zamakhshari said: "and his companion" is the devil appointed for him in His saying ﴿We appoint for him a devil, so he is his companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. Supporting this is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾, and ﴿This is what is ready with me﴾, meaning: this is something with me, and in my possession, ready for Hell. The meaning is: an angel drives him, and another bears witness against him, and a devil joined with him says: I have prepared him for Hell and made him ready for it by my seduction and misguidance. End of quote. This is the view of Mujahid. al-Hasan and Qatada also said: the angel who is a witness against him. al-Hasan also said: he is the recorder of his bad deeds. "Ma" is an indefinite described by the adverbial phrase and by ʿatīd, and relative (mawṣūla), with the adverbial phrase as its relative clause. As for ʿatīd, al-Zamakhshari said: it is a substitute (badal) or a second predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quote. The majority read ʿatīd with a raf (damma), and ʿAbd Allah read it with a nasb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and in that case it is better for "ما" to be relative.

﴿Cast into Hell﴾: the address is from Allah to the two angels, the driver and the witness. It is said: to two angels from the angels of punishment; in this case the alif is the dual pronoun. Mujahid and a group said: it is a statement, either to the driver or to the one who is among the guards, and as an address to one person. al-Mubarrad said its meaning is: "alqi, alqi" (cast, cast), and made it dual. al-Farra' said: it is from addressing one person with the address of two. It is said: the alif is a substitute for the light nun, making pausal form the connected form. These are statements that are disliked, and there is no necessity to depart from the apparent wording, according to Mujahid's view. al-Hasan read ﴿ألْقَيِنَ﴾ with the light nun of emphasis (nun al-tawkid al-khafifa), which is anomalous and contradicts the transmission by mass report (tawatur) with the alif. ﴿every stubborn disbeliever﴾: that is, one who denies the blessing and the Benefactor. ﴿ʿanīd﴾: Qatada said: deviating from obedience. al-Hasan said: obstinate and rebellious. al-Suddi said: the "masaq" from the root (ʿind), which is a bone that lodges in the throat. Ibn Bahr said: one who is pleased with what is in him.

﴿Hinderer of good﴾: Qatada, Mujahid and ʿIkrima said: it means the zakat. It is said: a miser. It is said: one who prevents his brother's sons from faith, like al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who used to say to them: whoever among you enters it, I will not benefit him with anything as long as I live. The better view is that the good is general, in wealth and other things. ﴿Doubter﴾: al-Hasan said: one who doubts Allah or the Resurrection. It is said: one who accuses. Those who allowed that it could be in the accusative as a substitute for "every disbeliever", and in the genitive as a substitute for "disbeliever", and in the nominative as the subject with the implicit meaning of a conditional, which is why the fa' entered its predicate, which is ﴿fa-alqiyahu﴾. The apparent is that it is connected to what precedes it by way of substitution, and that ﴿fa-alqiyahu﴾ is an emphasis (tawkid). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be a description from the point that "disbeliever" is specified by the mentioned attributes, so it is permissible to describe it with this definiteness. End of quote. This is nothing; if an indefinite is described by many attributes, it is not permissible to describe it with a definite.

﴿His companion says﴾: this sentence is not introduced with a waw, unlike ﴿and his companion says﴾ before it, because this one is resumed (istīnāf), just as sentences are resumed in the narration of the dialogue in the exchange of Moses and Pharaoh. So a dialogue happened between the disbeliever and his companion, as though the disbeliever said: "My Lord, it is he who made me transgress," and ﴿his companion says: Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾. As for ﴿and his companion says﴾, it is conjoined to show the combination of its meaning and the meaning of what precedes it in occurrence, namely the coming of every soul with the two angels. The statement of his companion is what he said to him. The meaning of ﴿I did not make him transgress﴾ is a declaration of his own innocence from having influenced him. ﴿But he was in far error﴾: that is, from himself, not from me. He is the one who preferred blindness over guidance, like His saying: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. He denied the companion, who had indeed made him transgress by his whispering and adornment.

﴿He says: Do not dispute before Me﴾: also a resumed statement like "he says" (qāla qarīnuhu), as though someone asked: what did Allah the Exalted say? So it was said: ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, that is, in the abode of recompense and the place of reckoning.

﴿And I had already presented to you the warning﴾: for those who disobeyed Me, so I left you no proof.

﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾: that is, with Me (ʿindi). Whatever I have decreed cannot be changed. al-Farra' said: what is not denied with Me, because of My knowledge of all matters. "Qaddamtu" (I had presented): it is permissible that [p. 127] it means "taqaddamtu" (I had advanced), that is, my statement to you has already preceded, joined with the warning; or it means "qaddama" as a transitive verb, and "bi-l-waʿīd" is the object, and the bā' is extra. The presenting was in the world, and their prohibition from disputing in the Hereafter; so the two times differ. Therefore the clause ﴿and I had already presented﴾ is not a circumstantial phrase except by interpretation, meaning: "and it has been established with you that I had presented," and the establishment of that is in the Hereafter; so the time of the prohibition from disputing agrees with the validity of the presenting, as a contemporaneous circumstance according to this interpretation.

﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾: the explanation of a similar phrase has already been given at the end of Al ʿImran. The meaning: I do not punish one who does not deserve punishment.

al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Nafiʿ, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Jaʿfar and al-Aʿmash read ﴿يَوْمَ يَقُولُ﴾ with the ya' of the third person, and the rest of the seven read with the nun. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash also read it in the passive form, "yuqal". The accusative of "yawm" is governed by "ẓallām" (unjust), or by "udhkur" (remember), or by "andhir" (warn), similarly. al-Zamakhshari said: it may be accusative governed by "nufikha" (it will be blown), as though it were said: "and the Trumpet will be blown on the Day We say..." and on this view "dhalika" refers to "yawma yaqulu". End of quote. This is very far, since on this view the governor and the governed are separated by many sentences, and this view does not suit the eloquence and rhetoric of the Qur'an. ﴿Have you been filled?﴾: is a confirmation and a questioning-to-stop, not a true question, because He, the Exalted, knows the conditions of Hell. It is said: this question and answer from it is literal. It is said: it is by omission of a modifier, that is, "We say to the keepers of Hell," as al-Rummani said. It is said: the question and answer are of the kind of depiction that establishes the meaning, that is, its condition is that of one who, if it spoke in reply to its questioner, would say such and such. This view shows that at that time it was not full. So its saying ﴿Is there any more?﴾ is a question and a desire for increase and for much from those entering it. al-Hasan, ʿAmr and Wasil said: it was full at the time of the question, so it does not increase beyond its fullness, as in the hadith: "Has ʿAqil left us any house?" meaning, what he left. ﴿Mazid﴾ may be a verbal noun or a passive participle.

﴿Not far off﴾: a place not far off, and it is an emphasis for ﴿was brought near﴾ [al-Takwir: 13]. It lifted the figurative nearness by the promise and the report. So the accusative of "ghayr" is adverbial, an adjective standing in the place of "makan" (place), so it takes its case. al-Zamakhshari permitted that "ghayr baʿid" be accusative as a circumstance of Paradise. He said: its masculine form, meaning "baʿid", is because it is on the pattern of a verbal noun, like "al-zaʾīr" and "al-ṣalīl", and verbal nouns are the same in describing masculine and feminine by them. End of quote. That it is on the pattern of a verbal noun does not permit a masculine to be an adjective of a feminine. al-Zamakhshari also said: or by omitting the described, that is, "something not far off". End of quote. It seems he meant "a not-far bringing near," and this is a reference to the reward.

The majority read ﴿مَا تُوعَدُونَ﴾ (what you are promised) with address to the believers, and Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read it with the ya' of the third person, meaning: this statement is what the promise was made of; and it is a parenthetical clause between the substituted-for and the substitute. ﴿For every constantly returning one﴾: this is the substitute for "al-muttaqin" (the God-fearing).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 50, verse 22–35 (part 2 of 2):

﴿مَن خَشِيَ﴾ (man khashiya, "whoever feared"): a second substitute (badal ba'da badal) following (li-kull, "for every"), as said by al-Zamakhshari. He made it a follower of (li-kull) rather than a substitute for (lil-muttaqin), because substitution does not repeat from a single substituted-for noun. He said: "It is permissible for it to be a substitute for the described noun of awwab (one who turns back in repentance) and hafiz (one who guards), but it is not permissible for it to be in the position of awwab and hafiz, because one who is not described by it is not described from among the rest of the relative pronouns except by alladhi." End of quote. He means by his words "in the position of awwab" that it be made a qualifier of it, and this is a correct judgment. As for his statement that it is not described from among the relative pronouns except by alladhi, the restriction is not correct: the Arabs have described with what has the definite article (al-) and is a relative pronoun, such as al-qa'im and al-mudrub, and they described with dhu al-Ta'iyyah, and dhat for the feminine. Among their speech: "bi-l-fadl dhu fadalakum Allahu bihi, wa-l-karamah dhat akramakumu Allahu bihi," meaning "by the favour with which Allah favoured you, and by the honour with which Allah honoured you." Al-Zamakhshari does not mean the specificity of alladhi, but rather its derivatives of the feminine, the dual and the plural, according to the differing dialects of these forms. He also permitted that man be a relative pronoun, a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted saying, its estimate being: "It will be said to them: enter it," because man has the sense of the plural. And that it be conditional, with the answer being the omitted verb, i.e., "then it will be said." And that it be a vocative, as in their saying: "man la yazalu muhsinan ahsin ilayya" (whoever ceases to be good, be good to me), and the particle of address is omitted for proximity. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that man is a qualifier." End of quote. This is not permissible, because man is not qualified by it. As for bi-l-ghayb (in the unseen), it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, i.e., while He is absent from him, and he only perceived Him by necessary knowledge, since every made thing must have a maker. It is also permissible that it be an attribute of the verbal noun of khashiya, i.e., he feared Him with a fear combined with the unseen, in that he feared His punishment while He was absent, or he feared Him because of the unseen which He threatened him with of His punishment. It was said: in seclusion, where no one sees him, in which case it is a circumstantial clause of the subject. And fear is paired with al-Rahman in view of the one who fears, since he knows that He is vast in mercy, and yet he fears Him.

﴿ادْخُلُوها بِسَلامٍ﴾ (udkhulu-ha bi-salam, "enter it in peace"): that is, safe from punishment, or greeted with peace by Allah and His angels.

﴿ذَلِكَ يَوْمُ الخُلُودِ﴾ (dhalika yawmu al-khulud, "that is the day of eternity"): like His saying: ﴿فادْخُلُوها خالِدِينَ﴾ ("enter it, abiding forever", Az-Zumar: 73), that is, presuming eternity. It is parallel to His saying concerning the disbelievers: ﴿ذَلِكَ يَوْمُ الوَعِيدِ﴾ ("that is the day of the threat", Qaf: 20).

﴿لَهم ما يَشاءُونَ فِيها﴾ (lahum ma yashaun fiha, "for them is whatever they wish therein"): that is, whatever their wills attach to, of kinds of pleasures and honours, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ولَكم فِيها ما تَشْتَهِي أنْفُسُكُمْ﴾ ("and for you therein is whatever your souls desire", Fussilat: 31).

﴿ولَدَيْنا مَزِيدٌ﴾ (wa-ladayna mazid, "and with Us is more"): an increase, or a thing added beyond what they wish. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿فَلا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ ما أُخْفِيَ لَهم مِن قُرَّةِ أعْيُنٍ﴾ ("no soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes", As-Sajdah: 17), and as came in the hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has it occurred to the heart of a human being, what I have revealed to them of it." And "mazid" is indefinite. It was said: the multiplication of a good deed tenfold. It was said: spouses from the houris of Paradise. It was said: Allah's manifestation to them until they see Him.

[p. 125] The Almighty and Majestic said: ﴿Certainly you were heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and today your sight is sharp.﴾ ﴿And his companion says, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever,﴾ ﴿hinderer of good, transgressor, doubter,﴾ ﴿who set up another god with Allah, so cast him into the severe punishment.﴾ ﴿His companion says, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error."﴾ ﴿He says, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning.﴾ ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants."﴾ ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Have you been filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ ﴿And Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, not far off.﴾ ﴿"This is what you were promised, for every constantly returning, watchful one,﴾ ﴿who feared the Most Merciful in the unseen and came with a heart turning in repentance.﴾ ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity."﴾ ﴿For them there is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more.﴾ ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in force, and they roamed through the lands; was there any escape?﴾ [Qaf: 36] ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 37] ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.﴾ [Qaf: 38] ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ [Qaf: 39] ﴿And glorify Him during part of the night and after the prostrations.﴾ [Qaf: 40] ﴿And listen on the Day the caller calls from a near place,﴾ [Qaf: 41] ﴿the Day they hear the Shout in truth; that is the Day of coming forth.﴾ [Qaf: 42] ﴿Indeed We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.﴾ [Qaf: 43] ﴿On the Day the earth splits open from them, hastening; that is a gathering easy for Us.﴾ [Qaf: 44] ﴿We know best what they say, and you are not over them a compeller. So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.﴾ [Qaf: 45] And (the commentary moves to) al-Dhariyat.

[p. 126] The majority of readers recited ﴿لَقَدْ كُنْتَ﴾ (kunta, "you were") with a fatha on the ta and the kaf in "كُنْتَ", and in "﴿غِطاءَكَ﴾" and "بَصَرُكَ", whereas al-Jahdari read them with a kasra, addressing the self (nafs). The majority read ﴿عَنْكَ غِطاءَكَ فَبَصَرُكَ﴾ with a fatha on the ta and the kaf, treating it according to the masculine wording of "كُلُّ" (every). Al-Jahdari and Talha ibn Musarrif read عَنْكِ غِطاءَكِ فَبَصَرُكِ with a kasra, also observing the feminine nafs. The author of al-Lawami' (Sahib al-Lawami') reported the kasra on the kaf only from Talha alone. He said: "I did not find it from him in ﴿لَقَدْ كُنْتَ﴾." If the kasra is read, then all of them are one form; and if ﴿لَقَدْ كُنْتَ﴾ is read with a fatha, then it is an interpretation by taking "كُلُّ" as masculine. It is permissible to make "كُلُّ" feminine in this construction because it is annexed to nafs, which is feminine. Even if that is so, he treated part of it according to the wording and part according to the meaning, like His saying: ﴿فَلَهُ أجْرُهُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112], then He said: ﴿وَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62]. End of quote.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Salih ibn Kaysan and al-Dahhak said: it is said to the disbelieving heedless one among those who have a soul accompanied by the driver and the witness, when he is brought before the Most Merciful and sees the realities which he did not believe in during the world and which he neglected to consider: ﴿Certainly you were heedless of this﴾, that is, of the consequence of disbelief. ﴿So when the covering is removed from you, your sight is sharp﴾, that is, your insight is sharp. This is like saying: so-and-so has a sharp mind (ḥadīd al-dhihn). Mujahid said: it is the sight of the eye, meaning his gaze became sharp toward his scale and other terrors of the Resurrection. There is a statement from Zayd ibn Aslam on this verse which it is forbidden to transmit, and it is in the book of Ibn ʿAtiyya. He used "the covering" as a metaphor for heedlessness, as though it covered all of him or his eyes, so he does not see. When he is in the Resurrection, heedlessness departs from him, and he sees what he did not see of the truth.

﴿And his companion says﴾: that is, among the guards of Hell. ﴿This﴾: the punishment that is with me for this disbelieving human. ﴿Ready﴾: present. This statement is made beautiful by the use of "ما" for what does not reason. Qatada said: "his companion" is the angel assigned to driving him, meaning: this disbeliever whom I drive is present with me. al-Zahrawi said: it is also said that "his companion" is his devil, but this is weak, because what is in it is that the companion in His saying ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾ is his devil in the world who misled him, without disagreement. The word "qarin" is a noun of genus, so his driver is a qarin, his companion among the guards is a qarin, and one who walks alongside a person on his path is a qarin. It is said: his companion here is his deed, in heart and limbs. al-Zamakhshari said: "and his companion" is the devil appointed for him in His saying ﴿We appoint for him a devil, so he is his companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. Supporting this is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾, and ﴿This is what is ready with me﴾, meaning: this is something with me, and in my possession, ready for Hell. The meaning is: an angel drives him, and another bears witness against him, and a devil joined with him says: I have prepared him for Hell and made him ready for it by my seduction and misguidance. End of quote. This is the view of Mujahid. al-Hasan and Qatada also said: the angel who is a witness against him. al-Hasan also said: he is the recorder of his bad deeds. "Ma" is an indefinite described by the adverbial phrase and by ʿatīd, and relative (mawṣūla), with the adverbial phrase as its relative clause. As for ʿatīd, al-Zamakhshari said: it is a substitute (badal) or a second predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quote. The majority read ʿatīd with a raf (damma), and ʿAbd Allah read it with a nasb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and in that case it is better for "ما" to be relative.

﴿Cast into Hell﴾: the address is from Allah to the two angels, the driver and the witness. It is said: to two angels from the angels of punishment; in this case the alif is the dual pronoun. Mujahid and a group said: it is a statement, either to the driver or to the one who is among the guards, and as an address to one person. al-Mubarrad said its meaning is: "alqi, alqi" (cast, cast), and made it dual. al-Farra' said: it is from addressing one person with the address of two. It is said: the alif is a substitute for the light nun, making pausal form the connected form. These are statements that are disliked, and there is no necessity to depart from the apparent wording, according to Mujahid's view. al-Hasan read ﴿ألْقَيِنَ﴾ with the light nun of emphasis (nun al-tawkid al-khafifa), which is anomalous and contradicts the transmission by mass report (tawatur) with the alif. ﴿every stubborn disbeliever﴾: that is, one who denies the blessing and the Benefactor. ﴿ʿanīd﴾: Qatada said: deviating from obedience. al-Hasan said: obstinate and rebellious. al-Suddi said: the "masaq" from the root (ʿind), which is a bone that lodges in the throat. Ibn Bahr said: one who is pleased with what is in him.

﴿Hinderer of good﴾: Qatada, Mujahid and ʿIkrima said: it means the zakat. It is said: a miser. It is said: one who prevents his brother's sons from faith, like al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who used to say to them: whoever among you enters it, I will not benefit him with anything as long as I live. The better view is that the good is general, in wealth and other things. ﴿Doubter﴾: al-Hasan said: one who doubts Allah or the Resurrection. It is said: one who accuses. Those who allowed that it could be in the accusative as a substitute for "every disbeliever", and in the genitive as a substitute for "disbeliever", and in the nominative as the subject with the implicit meaning of a conditional, which is why the fa' entered its predicate, which is ﴿fa-alqiyahu﴾. The apparent is that it is connected to what precedes it by way of substitution, and that ﴿fa-alqiyahu﴾ is an emphasis (tawkid). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be a description from the point that "disbeliever" is specified by the mentioned attributes, so it is permissible to describe it with this definiteness. End of quote. This is nothing; if an indefinite is described by many attributes, it is not permissible to describe it with a definite.

﴿His companion says﴾: this sentence is not introduced with a waw, unlike ﴿and his companion says﴾ before it, because this one is resumed (istīnāf), just as sentences are resumed in the narration of the dialogue in the exchange of Moses and Pharaoh. So a dialogue happened between the disbeliever and his companion, as though the disbeliever said: "My Lord, it is he who made me transgress," and ﴿his companion says: Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾. As for ﴿and his companion says﴾, it is conjoined to show the combination of its meaning and the meaning of what precedes it in occurrence, namely the coming of every soul with the two angels. The statement of his companion is what he said to him. The meaning of ﴿I did not make him transgress﴾ is a declaration of his own innocence from having influenced him. ﴿But he was in far error﴾: that is, from himself, not from me. He is the one who preferred blindness over guidance, like His saying: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. He denied the companion, who had indeed made him transgress by his whispering and adornment.

﴿He says: Do not dispute before Me﴾: also a resumed statement like "he says" (qāla qarīnuhu), as though someone asked: what did Allah the Exalted say? So it was said: ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, that is, in the abode of recompense and the place of reckoning.

﴿And I had already presented to you the warning﴾: for those who disobeyed Me, so I left you no proof.

﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾: that is, with Me (ʿindi). Whatever I have decreed cannot be changed. al-Farra' said: what is not denied with Me, because of My knowledge of all matters. "Qaddamtu" (I had presented): it is permissible that [p. 127] it means "taqaddamtu" (I had advanced), that is, my statement to you has already preceded, joined with the warning; or it means "qaddama" as a transitive verb, and "bi-l-waʿīd" is the object, and the bā' is extra. The presenting was in the world, and their prohibition from disputing in the Hereafter; so the two times differ. Therefore the clause ﴿and I had already presented﴾ is not a circumstantial phrase except by interpretation, meaning: "and it has been established with you that I had presented," and the establishment of that is in the Hereafter; so the time of the prohibition from disputing agrees with the validity of the presenting, as a contemporaneous circumstance according to this interpretation.

﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾: the explanation of a similar phrase has already been given at the end of Al ʿImran. The meaning: I do not punish one who does not deserve punishment.

al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Nafiʿ, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Jaʿfar and al-Aʿmash read ﴿يَوْمَ يَقُولُ﴾ with the ya' of the third person, and the rest of the seven read with the nun. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash also read it in the passive form, "yuqal". The accusative of "yawm" is governed by "ẓallām" (unjust), or by "udhkur" (remember), or by "andhir" (warn), similarly. al-Zamakhshari said: it may be accusative governed by "nufikha" (it will be blown), as though it were said: "and the Trumpet will be blown on the Day We say..." and on this view "dhalika" refers to "yawma yaqulu". End of quote. End of quote. It seems he meant "a not-far bringing near," and this is a reference to the reward.

Similar to it is His saying: ﴿فَلا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ ما أُخْفِيَ لَهم مِن قُرَّةِ أعْيُنٍ﴾ ("no soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes", As-Sajdah: 17), and as came in the hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has it occurred to the heart of a human being, what I have revealed to them of it."
